Both numbers are now worked out wherever they are shown, from the copies published and the copies claimed, so a sold out drop reads as sold out and a meter never shows a word where a number belongs.

  • The website demo's own badge stays off the app's controls

    Opened on a phone, the green "live demo" pill and the download prompt sat exactly where the dashboard puts its bar of buttons, covering the first of them, and the pill also covered the buttons of any dialog that opened over it. Both now sit above the bar, only one of them appears at a time, and the pill steps aside while a dialog is open.

  • Xenon tells you when the file index has run out of room, and which folder it left out

    The index that search and the Disk space widget read has a safety limit on how many files it holds, so it cannot grow without bound on your RAM. Point it at whole drives and that limit is reachable: past it, Xenon stops adding files. The Disk space widget already said so, but Settings under Search, the one place you can do something about it, showed only the file count, which reads as everything having worked. It now says the limit was reached, names the folders that were left out, and tells you that removing one from the list or naming a precise folder instead of a whole drive is the fix. Nothing about the limit itself has changed.

  • A file you delete no longer stays in the index forever after that limit is hit

    The index removes entries for files that are gone by re-reading a folder and dropping what it no longer finds. That step was correctly skipped when a read had been cut short, because a partial read is not evidence a file is gone, but the check asked whether the index had *ever* hit its limit rather than whether *this* read was cut short. So the first time any folder reached the limit, removal switched off permanently, for every folder, and deleted files accumulated in the index from then on. Search still refused to open anything that was really gone, so nothing wrong ever happened, but results filled up with names that no longer exist. The check now asks about the read in front of it.

4.11.4 10 August 2026

Added

  • The buttons in the top bar are yours to arrange

    Lock, Ambient, Xenon, Search, Layout, Apps and the favourite apps can each be hidden, dragged into the order you want, and moved to the left or the right side. It works the same in the full bar and in the Dynamic Island's side rails, so it does not depend on which of the two you use. Until now the only way to get rid of a button you never press was to close a whole rail, which took the others with it, or to switch the bar off entirely, which did not remove the buttons at all, it just moved them.

    The list is in Settings, under Dynamic Island, below the island elements. Two buttons always stay: Settings and Layout. They are the way back in rather than features, one undoes anything, the other lets you rearrange the dashboard again, and on a touchscreen with no keyboard, hiding either would leave no way to open it. Their eyes are there but greyed out with the reason on them. In exchange they now sit back visually: no plate, no outline, dimmed until you touch them, so the buttons you actually chose to keep are the ones that stand out. The Layout button comes back to full strength while you are editing, since that is a mode worth seeing.

  • An empty side rail no longer leaves its arrow behind

    In the Dynamic Island's minimal chrome, moving every button to one side left the other rail as a lone arrow that opened an empty capsule. A rail with nothing in it now goes away entirely, and comes back the moment something lands in it, a button moved over, an app you star, or a widget drawing into the mini slot. It can never take both rails with it, since Settings and Layout cannot be hidden.

  • The clock is centred again when you strip the bar down

    With the date, the weather and the music hidden, the row under the time still held the small connection dot, and the clock is centred as a block, so the time sat 5.5px above the middle of the bar and read as crooked. The dot keeps its place under the digits, but it no longer pushes them up.

  • The space you free can hold something

    A widget can now draw a small readout among the buttons, a temperature, a count, a meter, with one button you can press, in the position you put it. It is drawn by Xenon rather than by the widget, like the island and the badges, so nothing about how widgets are sandboxed changes. You choose which side it sits on, you can hide it, and you can switch any single widget's contribution off on its own.

  • Everything a widget puts in the bar is listed in one place, with a switch each

    Whether it writes a line in the island, a chip next to the clock or a mini widget among the buttons, the extension shows up in Settings under Dynamic Island with what it adds and a switch to turn it off, without uninstalling it. That list existed but only ever said "island", so a widget sitting somewhere else in the bar was hard to connect to it.

  • One button puts the whole bar back

    It resets the style, the island elements, the button layout, the side rails, the clock format, and switches every extension back on. It now asks first: it undoes an arrangement you may have spent time on, and there is no way back from it.

  • Badges next to the clock can be tapped

    They were display-only. A widget can now ask for its badge to be a button, and it is a permission you grant separately from the badge itself, so a widget that could only show you a number cannot quietly become one you can press after an update.

  • Your dashboard pages can have names, and the dots at the top can show them

    Until now the pages were a row of identical dots: nothing told you which one held your music and which one held your PC stats, and you found out by swiping. In Layout mode there is now a pencil button next to the page controls that names the page you are on, and a switch in Settings under Dynamic Island, on the "Page dots" row, turns those dots into buttons carrying the names. It works in the normal top bar and in the island, so it does not depend on which of the two you use.

    The switch is off to begin with, so nothing changes for a dashboard you have already arranged. A long name is shortened to fit rather than pushing the bar wider, and clearing the name field puts the page back to the name it started with instead of leaving it blank.

Fixed

  • The weather tile no longer empties for good until you reload the dashboard

    After a while it went blank and stayed blank, however long you left it, while the weather itself was perfectly available, opening the same address in a browser at that exact moment returned the forecast. Only reloading the page by hand brought it back, and then it happened again.

    The cause is that a request to fetch the weather had no time limit. Almost always it answers in a moment, but if one ever hangs, a sleep and resume, a hiccup in the network stack, it never finishes and never fails either. Xenon skips a refresh while the previous one is still going, so a request that never ends means every later refresh is skipped too, for as long as the page stays open. On a dashboard left running for days, it only has to happen once. Requests now have a deadline, so a stuck one is abandoned and the next refresh goes ahead normally.

    The same gap existed in the readings for system, network and audio, and is closed there too. And when a refresh does fail, the tile now keeps the last forecast and marks it as not current, instead of throwing it away: one from a few minutes ago is still worth reading. Past three hours old it stops pretending and tells you what went wrong. Reported on Discord.

  • The weather no longer depends on one single service being reachable

    To ask for a forecast Xenon first has to know where you are, and in automatic mode it got that from one address on the internet. If your PC could not reach that one address, and a DNS blocker, a router filter, an antivirus web filter or a company network is enough to do it, then nothing said so: the two good forecast services need coordinates and were skipped without a word, and the whole feature quietly fell back to the third and least reliable one. It kept working, with the coarser data and the odd "next hours" line that came with it, until the day that last service was busy too and the tile went blank.

    Xenon now asks a second and a third source when the first does not answer, so one blocked address is no longer enough to take the weather down. Nothing changes when the first one works: it is asked, it answers, and the others are never contacted.

  • A weather tile that cannot show anything now says why

    It used to say "Weather unavailable" and stop there, which is the same sentence for three completely different problems: your position could not be determined, the city you typed does not exist, or the weather services did not answer. Only one of them is fixable by you, and there was no way to tell which one you had. The tile now names the cause, and the details panel adds a line on what to do about it: check the connection or a blocker, try a nearby city name, or simply wait for the next refresh. In all eleven languages.

  • The YouTube and Twitch widgets now tell you they need an account, instead of sitting there empty

    With no account connected, both tiles took all their contents off screen and left the logo on an empty background. Nothing said why, nothing offered a way forward, and the tile looked identical to one that had broken. It was most confusing in layout editing mode, which forces the contents back into view: the widget appeared to work there and appeared broken everywhere else, which reads like a display fault rather than a setting.

    Each tile now shows one line saying the account has to be connected, and tapping it opens the page where you connect it. This covers the YouTube watching widget, the YouTube Live widget and the Twitch watching widget. The YouTube Live tile had that line already, but it lived inside the panel that gets hidden, so it disappeared at exactly the moment it was the only thing worth saying.

  • Those widgets no longer say "Loading…" over an answer they already have

    The video and channel lists showed the loading line for two different situations: the check for a connected account still being in flight, and that check having come back with a definite no. The second one never resolves, so the list sat on "Loading…" indefinitely on a dashboard where nothing was actually loading. A definite no now says the account is not connected.

  • Five languages showed one of those messages in English

    Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Russian had no translation for the "connect in Settings" line used by the Discord widget, so it fell back to English while the identical line in the YouTube widget right next to it was translated. All the new text here is available in all 11 languages.

  • Xenon no longer opens in the shape of a screen you may not own

    On a PC with no CORSAIR Xeneon Edge attached, the app opened as a window with that 14.5" panel's own 3.556:1 proportions, up to 1600×450, whatever monitor you actually have. On an ordinary screen that is a wide slot across the middle with desktop showing above and below it, and it was the first thing you saw after installing. The window now opens at the size of the screen hosting it: that monitor's own proportions, at 88% of it, centred. Where an Edge *is* attached nothing changes, that panel is still taken over whole, which is the point of it.

    Two quieter versions of the same mistake went with it. The window was built at 2560×720 before anything resized it, which is the Edge's exact resolution, and on macOS, where it cannot be created full-screen, that first frame was what you got. And it was created full-screen on every machine and then immediately shrunk, so opening Xenon covered your entire desktop for a moment and then did not. It is now built at the size it is going to keep, and full-screen only where a real Edge is waiting for it.

  • The first question Xenon asks now has your screens in it

    On first run it asks whether the dashboard should live on this PC or on your phone or tablet, and the "on this PC" side is meant to list your monitors so you can say which one. That list only arrived with the first update the app sends the page after the dashboard has finished loading, so the question could open with no screens on it, and if that update never landed, it stayed that way: a question about which screen to use, asked without offering one. The screens are now handed to the page before it loads, so they are there from the first frame, and they still redraw the moment a monitor is plugged in or out.

    And a screen can now be picked whatever your system calls it, which, on two of the three platforms, was not a given. On Linux an output the system has no model string for had no identity to save, so the tray menu left it out of "Show on" altogether and the picker drew it as a button that refused to be pressed: the screen was listed and could not be chosen, and on a machine where nothing is named the question had no answer at all. On macOS the opposite problem: every screen is named, but the name is the display's model number, so two identical monitors, the ordinary way to own two, were the same screen as far as Xenon was concerned. Both showed as the primary one, the tray offered two entries that did the same thing, and choosing the second one moved the window to the first, quietly and for good. A screen is now identified by where it is when its name cannot tell it apart from another.

    One limit worth knowing on Linux: under Wayland a window is not allowed to place itself, so which screen it opens on is the compositor's decision, not Xenon's. The choice is saved either way, and it is honoured on Windows, on macOS and on X11.

4.11.3 6 August 2026

Added

  • macOS stops forgetting Xenon's permissions every time it updates

    This is the cause of most of what is fixed below, and it had been true since the Mac build shipped. macOS ties a permission, Full Disk Access above all, to the app's code signature, and Xenon's signature was generated fresh at every build. So every release looked to macOS like a completely different app, and everything you had allowed silently stopped applying: the switch in System Settings still showed as on, and did nothing, because that list shows a name while macOS compares a signature.

    Xenon now carries its own certificate, which stays the same from one release to the next, so a permission granted once keeps working. The update to this version resets it one final time, since this is the release where the identity changes: grant it again here and you should not have to think about it after that. Two honest notes. This does not remove the warning macOS shows the first time you open Xenon, that needs Apple's paid notarization, which this project still does not have. And the certificate is Xenon's own rather than Apple-issued, which is exactly why it is free and why it is enough for this particular problem.

Fixed

  • No more storm of permission requests on a Mac

    When the permission above had lapsed, Xenon's file index kept trying to read your home folder anyway, so macOS asked for the Desktop, then Documents, then Downloads, then Photos, then Music, and asked again on the next pass, and the next. It made the machine genuinely hard to use, and nothing on screen connected it to Xenon having lost a permission after an update.

    Xenon now checks whether the permission is really in force, and while it is not it simply stays out of your home folder rather than knocking on every protected door in it. Instead you get one notice that says what happened, with a button that opens the right settings pane, it is buried four levels deep and named differently on each macOS version, so pointing at it beats describing it. A folder you picked yourself is still indexed: you chose that one. And when you grant the permission, search and the disk map come back on their own within a minute, with nothing to restart.

  • Buttons on notifications did nothing

    Any notification offering a choice, the one above, and the update notice's "Skip this version", swallowed the tap: the card's swipe-to-dismiss gesture captured it before the button saw it. Worse on the update notice, where the tap fell through to the card's own action, so declining a version installed it instead.

  • The first install on a Mac now ends with the dashboard on screen, instead of a spinner and an error

    With 4.11.2 the setup finally ran to the end, it downloaded Xenon, installed it, registered it to start at login, and then nothing started it. The window reported that the dashboard had not answered, and the app kept turning on "Waiting for the Xenon service" forever, on an installation that had actually succeeded. Quitting Xenon and opening it again fixed it, which is not something anyone should have to guess.

    The reason is that the piece which starts the dashboard is Xenon itself, and Xenon was already open, it is what opened the setup window in the first place. It looks for a dashboard once, when it launches, and at that moment there was nothing installed yet to find. The command that starts Xenon at login does nothing when Xenon is already running, so no one ever asked it to look again. The installer now closes and reopens the app itself once the install is done, so that second look happens. Xenon holds the dashboard on a Mac on purpose: started that way it inherits the app's Full Disk Access, which is what lets the Disk widget and search see the Trash and your caches.

4.11.2 6 August 2026

Fixed

  • Installing Xenon on a Mac from the .dmg now finishes

    The app opened, the setup window appeared, it found the release, downloaded it and verified its signature, and then stopped on the line right before it started copying anything, with INSTALL_ROOT: unbound variable. The window closed itself, nothing was installed, and the app sat on "Waiting for the Xenon service..." forever. There was no way to tell from the outside that anything had gone wrong.

    The cause was one missing pair of braces. macOS still ships bash 3.2, released in 2007, and that version reads the bytes of the … character glued to the end of a variable name as part of the name, so a message meant to say "Installing to <folder>…" asked for a variable that does not exist, and the script is set to stop dead rather than continue on an empty path. Every other shell, including the one on Linux and the one your Terminal opens by default, handles it correctly, which is why it only ever happened on a Mac.

  • Uninstalling on a Mac now works too, in v4.11.1 it stopped before removing anything

    The same line was in the uninstaller, at the point where it stops the running dashboard, so on a Mac it quit right there: no app removed, no login item removed, nothing. If you ran it and Xenon was still on your machine afterwards, that is why, run it again from this version and it will finish the job. A test now refuses to let that shape of line back into any script in the project, and every shipped script was checked against the shell macOS actually runs them with.

4.11.1 6 August 2026

Fixed

  • Uninstalling on macOS and Linux now actually uninstalls Xenon

    It stopped the backend and removed the startup entry, and then printed a list of the things it had deliberately left behind: the app, the folder, your data. That list made sense to whoever wrote it and to nobody else. What you saw was an uninstaller that finished, a Xenon icon still sitting in Applications, and Xenon still coming up when you searched for it, so the reasonable conclusion was that it had not worked. Worse, opening that leftover app re-registered its own start-at-login entry, so a machine you thought was clean started Xenon again at the next sign-in.

    It now removes Xenon: the app itself, wherever it is. On macOS every copy of Xenon.app is found by its identity rather than by its name, unregistered from the system's app database first, that database is what Spotlight, Launchpad and "Open with" actually read, and it keeps its entry for an app that was only deleted, which is why a Xenon dragged to the Trash could still be found and opened. On Linux the .deb/.rpm package, any AppImage in the folders people keep them in, and the launcher entries that put the icon in the app menu. Then the login items, the local server, the browser windows Xenon had opened, your data and the install folder itself, matching what UNINSTALL.bat has done on Windows since v4.4.0.

    Because it now deletes rather than keeps, it asks first: it lists exactly what is about to go and waits for you to type REMOVE. --keep-data keeps your settings, layouts and notes (and the folder they live in), --keep-files keeps just the folder, --dry-run shows you the whole list and changes nothing, and --yes skips the question in a script. --purge-data still works and is now simply what happens anyway. All three uninstallers also leave a folder alone when it is a git checkout rather than an install, that is somebody's working copy, with branches and unpushed commits in it.

    And on macOS the Terminal window closes itself when it is done. Terminal leaves a finished window on screen saying "[Process completed]", which after an uninstall reads as if something is still running, and left the very last thing on your screen being a window belonging to the app you had just removed.

  • The macOS installer window now shows you what to do with it

    Opening the .dmg gave you a plain window with the Xenon app sitting to the *right* of the Applications folder, so the drag everyone knows read backwards, at whatever size and spacing Finder felt like, and anyone who has hidden files visible also got the volume's icon file in there. The window had no layout at all because the tool that builds the image skips that step, by a flag whose own description says it produces "a DMG without any custom background or icons positioning". The layout is now decided once and carried inside the image itself, rather than asking the build machine to arrange it in Finder, which needs a desktop session no build server has, and which fails the whole build when it goes wrong. App on the left, Applications on the right, drag from one to the other.

  • Opening Xenon for the first time on a Mac could install nothing at all, in silence

    A .dmg cannot run an installer, so the first launch opens a Terminal window that sets the backend up. macOS has no way to hand a command to Terminal: it starts a window, starts a shell in it, and *types* the command at that shell, and if the shell is still starting, what arrives is garbled. Seen in the wild as command not found: o. The window opened, did nothing, and Xenon sat on "Waiting for the Xenon service…" forever, with nothing anywhere to say why. The app now waits for the setup to confirm it really started and opens the window once more if it did not.

  • The YouTube widget now tells you when a video will not play, instead of leaving YouTube's own error on screen

    Some videos cannot be played outside YouTube itself. That is a decision of whoever owns the video or the music inside it, not of Xenon, which is why videos from a channel you follow can work while others from that same channel do not, and why all of them still play fine on YouTube. Xenon already knew about this case and offered to open the video in your browser, but the offer was a line of text below the controls, while YouTube's own "Video unavailable" rectangle stayed sitting over the whole picture. So the only thing you actually saw was the error, and it looked like the widget was broken. Now the explanation and the Open in the browser button are drawn over the picture, in place of that rectangle.

    There was also a case where nothing was said at all: when YouTube refuses a video, what it puts in the frame is a plain error page, and that page cannot talk to Xenon. If that happened, the widget waited for a player that was never coming and left the black box there. It now gives that wait a deadline and shows the same explanation.

    And the list now says which videos those are, before you tap them. Finding out one tap at a time is tiring, and a playlist of live sets or DJ mixes can be mostly made of them. YouTube says so up front, in the same request that already fetches how long each video is, so it costs nothing extra: those videos carry a small YouTube only tag in the list, and tapping one takes you straight to your browser instead of starting a player that was going to refuse.

    Playing a whole list works again as well. Tapping a video plays everything after it, and one video that will not play used to stop the lot. Marked videos are left out of that queue, so a playlist plays the ones it can.

  • The YouTube widget was still in English for five languages

    Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Russian never had translations, so anyone using Xenon in one of them got the whole widget in English: the tabs, the player controls, the live broadcasting panel and every message it can show. All of it is translated now.

4.11.0 5 August 2026

New

  • The Claude Code widget now mirrors what is actually happening in the session, and every control on it does something real

    The tile could tell you a session was busy and very little else, and in three places it showed a control that did nothing. The worst was the question card: when Claude asked you to choose between options, the card showed the question and the options, the options could not be tapped, and the one button on it just made the card go away. Nothing reached the session. It is now a real question, tap an option and answer, and Claude carries on with your choice instead of waiting at the keyboard. Multiple-choice questions accept several answers, and there is still a button to leave it to the terminal if that is where you would rather answer it.

    You can write to a session that is still working. Typing to a session you had open started a separate run in the background, which is not what it looked like it was doing. Now, if that session is mid-turn, your message is queued and delivered to that same conversation the moment the current turn ends, the tile says so while it waits, and there is a Cancel next to it. If the session is idle instead, there is no turn left to end, so Xenon continues the conversation as a background run and says that too. The composer tells you which of the two is about to happen before you press send.

    The tile shows Claude's plan, ticking over. When Claude is working through a checklist, the widget shows that checklist: how many steps are done, which one is running now, and what is next. "It is busy" is what every other tool tells you; where it has got to is the thing worth having on a screen across the room.

    What it is doing, and what it is waiting for, are said out loud. A working session used to read "Bash", now it reads the actual command, and how long it has been on it, so a build and a hang stop looking identical. A session waiting on you used to say only "waiting for you"; it now says what for. Sub-agents show as their own chips instead of making one session look stuck. A conversation being compacted says so, rather than its context gauge collapsing for no visible reason. And a session that finished says whether it finished, was cleared, or was closed, instead of vanishing from the list and leaving you to guess.

    A session that is gone, goes. Closing Claude Code with Ctrl-C tells nothing to anyone, so the widget kept showing that session as live for a full hour, offering a follow-up nothing would ever deliver. Xenon now reads Claude Code's own list of running sessions and drops one the moment its process is gone. The same list means a session you started before Xenon was open shows up at all, which it previously did not.

    Clawd lives in the top bar now. The marker used to be a pill spelling its state out in words next to the clock, which is not where anyone reads a sentence, "wants your OK" spent six characters saying what a shape says at a glance. It is Claude Code's own pixel mascot instead, and it acts out what your sessions are doing: it walks while Claude is working, stands still and blinks when a session has finished and you have not looked yet, and hops twice and waits when Claude is blocked on you, with a small amber dot beside it. A number appears when more than one session is running, the words are still there if you hover, and it takes no space at all when nothing is happening.

    That last state is the one exception to Xenon's rule that everything stops moving when the screen goes quiet. A dialog on top, a minute without touches, game mode and Performance Mode all exist to stop decoration, and Clawd waiting for you is not decoration: it is the only thing on the bar that means a person is needed. Leaving it frozen made the one thing that wanted attention the one thing that held still. It keeps hopping through all four, and stops the moment you answer. If you have asked your system for reduced motion, none of it moves at all.

    And it no longer says a finished session is waiting for you. Claude Code sends the same kind of notification for two opposite things: "Claude needs your permission" while it is mid-task, and "Claude is waiting for your input" a minute after a turn has ended, which only means the prompt is empty. Xenon treated both as being blocked, so a session that had been finished for three quarters of an hour was drawn as waiting for you, and the top bar went to its loudest state over it while two other sessions were actually working. The two are now told apart by when they arrive rather than by reading their wording, which is a different sentence in every language and every version. A session that has finished stays finished.

    Two more fixes that came with it: a session that stopped to ask your permission was announced as having *finished answering*, the opposite of what happened, at the one moment the difference matters, and a promotional card from the Store could draw itself on top of an unanswered permission prompt. Settings → Claude Code has a second switch, next to the one for permissions, for whether questions are answered on this screen; both stay on unless you change them. All of it is translated into the 11 languages.

  • Wave Link works again, and the mixer tile is a real one now

    Wave Link 3 arrived in March and replaced the way other programs talk to it, so every Xenon build until now reported "Wave Link app not running" while the app was plainly running. Three things had changed at once. It no longer sits on a fixed port: it writes the port it picked into a file, and that number is different every time it starts, so no amount of searching would ever have found it. It expects a connecting program to introduce itself in a particular way, and refuses everything else outright. And it renamed the fields it uses to say who it is, so even a connection that worked would have been thrown away as "this is not Wave Link". Xenon now speaks both versions and tells you which one answered.

    The tile follows your own mixes. Wave Link 3 lets you create mixes and name them, and you can have as many as you like. The tabs across the top are those mixes, whatever you called them, however many there are. The old tile had a fixed Stream and Local pair, which on a Wave Link 3 rig would have shown two tabs for a setup with three and quietly hidden the rest. On Wave Link 2 you still get Local and Stream, because that is what that version has.

    Live stereo level meters, per channel. A thin two-bar meter under each fader, left and right separately so a dead side is visible rather than averaged away. They stop when the dashboard is idle, in game mode or behind a dialog, and they are only asked for while a dashboard is actually open, so nothing is metering into an empty room.

    The effect chain and the output are on the tile too. Each channel shows its effects as pills you tap to switch on and off, and the bottom row picks which pair of speakers or headphones the main mix comes out of. There are new Deck keys for all of it: mix volume, mute a mix, toggle an effect, switch the output device.

    The Deck keys you already made keep working. A key set up against Wave Link 2 stores "stream" or "local", and those keep meaning the stream mix and the personal mix against a Wave Link 3 mixer. Nothing needs reconfiguring. A key pointing at a mix you have since deleted now fails and says so, instead of moving the nearest fader.

    Found by two people on Discord who ran five rounds of diagnostics on their own machines, one of whom had already worked out half the protocol. tools/wavelink-probe.mjs is the read-only diagnostic that came out of it, and it now identifies both versions and says exactly what a refusal means.

  • Your phone's contacts, call history and keypad are on the dashboard now

    Pair a phone to the PC over Bluetooth, switch on Settings → Telefono associato, and a new Telefono tile shows who called and when, with received, dialled and missed told apart; your whole address book, searchable; and a keypad that places a real call through the phone. It reads the phone the same way a car does, over the standard Bluetooth profiles, so it works with an iPhone and with an Android and needs nothing installed on the phone itself. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the contacts are read on demand, kept on the PC, and never written to disk. It is off until you turn it on, because switching it on means reading your entire address book off your phone.

    A call now announces itself as a fact instead of a guess. Until now the incoming-call card noticed a phone call by reading the text of a mirrored notification and matching it against phrases in 11 languages, which means it could miss a call whose wording it did not recognise and, occasionally, fire on a message that merely mentioned one. For a phone call it now uses the operating system's own signal, so the card appears when the phone rings and goes when the call is over, and the notification is left to do the one thing it is genuinely good at: saying who is calling. The two no longer produce two cards for one call.

    Your messages are there too, and you can reply from the keyboard you are already typing on. The tile has a Messaggi tab: who wrote, when, what it says, and a reply box that sends a real message from your own number. Answering a text without picking the phone up is the thing this replaces, and it works the same way with an iPhone and an Android. The text is hidden until you tap it, and that is on by default rather than a preference nobody finds: an inbox is where one-time login codes arrive, and a dashboard sits on a desk in the open. You can switch the masking off in Settings if it is your own desk. Sending always asks first and shows you the message it is about to send, because a text cannot be recalled.

    One honest limit on Windows: "Collegamento al telefono" and Xenon cannot both hold the message connection. There is one channel and that app takes it whenever it runs, relaunching itself the moment your phone does anything. Xenon will not take it away from software you are also using, so if that app is open the Messaggi tab says the connection is busy instead of fighting for it. Close it and messages work. Contacts, call history and calling are not affected.

    What it cannot do, and why, is written on the settings panel rather than left for you to discover. You cannot answer or hang up a call from the dashboard. The Bluetooth channel that would accept a call is held by the operating system itself, and there is no public way to ask it to, so there is no Answer button rather than one that does nothing. Placing a call works; answering one does not. Calling and texting from a paired phone or tablet are deliberately not possible either: a call's audio comes out of the PC, so one started from another room would be a call nobody could hear, and a message sent from a device you might lose goes out under your own number. Reading everything from a paired device works normally.

  • You can send photos and files straight from your phone to this PC, and back

    Getting a photo off your phone has meant sending it to yourself in a messaging app, opening that app's website on the PC, and downloading it again. Now, once your phone is paired, open Xenon on it, tap Foto e video or Altri file, pick what you want, and the files land in Download/Xenon on your PC with their own names. It works the other way too: drag a file onto the tile from Explorer or Finder, and download it from your phone. Everything goes over your own network, never through anyone's server. The folder they land in is yours to change, in Settings → Telefono, and only from the PC. If a name is already taken Xenon adds a number and never replaces a file you already had. Photos are not re-encoded and not resized, so what arrives is what you took. A new Trasferimento file tile shows what has come and gone; on a phone there is also a button in the bottom bar, so you do not have to put the tile on your layout to use it. Two things worth knowing, and Xenon says both where you would otherwise find out the hard way: on an iPhone you have to open Xenon to send something, because iOS does not let any website appear in its Share button, and a file you download on an iPhone goes to the Files app rather than the camera roll. One file goes at a time, and if you close Xenon in the middle of a large video, that video starts over.

  • Xenon now asks which screen you want it on, the first time it opens

    Until now it never asked, and the answer it gave itself was invisible: with a Xeneon Edge attached it took the Edge, and without one it opened a window on your main monitor. The only way to change that was a submenu in the tray icon that almost nobody finds, and which was greyed out entirely if you owned an Edge. Now a short screen appears once, listing the displays it can actually see, with the Edge already selected if you have one. Pick a different screen and it stays there: your choice wins over the Edge, which it could not before. Pick my phone or tablet and, from the next start onwards, this PC shows nothing at all, no window, no icon, and at login only the background service starts, which is what serves the dashboard to your phone. It does not vanish the moment you choose: the window you are looking at is the one carrying the pairing QR code, so it stays until you are done, and it only takes effect once a phone is actually paired. Choosing it takes you straight to the pairing panel and turns nothing on by itself; that switch stays yours. There is a Decide later if you would rather not think about it, and it never asks twice. Everything is in Settings → Schermo afterwards, in all 11 languages, with the same list of displays and a full-screen switch. And if the screen you chose is unplugged, the window stays hidden instead of reappearing somewhere you never asked for; it comes back on its own when you plug it in, and Settings says so rather than leaving you wondering where Xenon went.

  • A widget does not have to be a rectangle any more

    Every tile on the dashboard has been a rounded rectangle since the first version, which is fine for a system monitor and quietly limiting for everything else: a clock, a pet, a hero stat, a piece of art. Open a tile's 🎨 style editor and there is now a Shape picker in the new Effects tab, with eleven silhouettes to choose from: squircle, circle, hexagon, diamond, cut corner, slant, ticket, arch, shield, wave and blob. The tile keeps its place in the grid, so nothing moves around it. The border follows the outline instead of the old rectangle, and Xenon works out how far the content has to stay from the cut edges and applies that margin itself, so a hexagon does not eat the end of every line of text. You can also write your own shape: paste any closed SVG path drawn in a 0 to 1 square and the tile takes it. If the path cannot be used, the editor says why instead of quietly doing nothing. A shape is saved with your layout, travels in a shared page or preset code, and works on the Xeneon Edge, in the app, in a browser and on a paired phone.

  • A widget can turn one person in a voice call up or down

    Discord lets you set the volume of a single person, per person, and mute them just for you, the two controls you reach for when one friend is twice as loud as everyone else. Both are now available to widgets, alongside the list of who is in your channel with the volume and local-mute state of each, so a widget can show a row per person with a slider that does the real thing. It is part of the existing "Control Discord voice" permission and needs Discord running. Documented for creators in the Widget SDK.

  • And a widget you install can arrive with its own shape

    A creator can declare the silhouette of their own tile in the widget's manifest ("shape": { "preset": "hexagon" }, or their own path), so a widget designed as a circle looks like a circle the moment it is installed rather than needing you to go and set it. This is not a permission and there is nothing to approve: a shape only ever affects that widget's own tile, it cannot touch anything else on your dashboard, and if you pick a shape for that tile yourself, yours wins. Widgets are told the shape they are in so they can lay themselves out around it. It is documented for creators in the Widget SDK, along with the eleven presets and the rules for a custom path.

  • Three of the per-tile effects were doing nothing at all, and now do what they say

    In the tile style editor, Glass blur and Glass saturation were writing settings that no part of a dashboard tile ever read, so moving those sliders changed nothing on any theme. Blur is now real: the tile blurs what is behind it, which on a photo background is the difference between a card and a pane of glass. It is only applied to tiles that ask for it, because blurring every tile costs graphics work on a screen that is on all day. Blur is also only visible through a panel you can see through, so the editor now says that on the spot instead of leaving you with a slider that appears broken. Panel shadow was the same story twice over: the value went into a setting nothing consumed, and the shadow was being cut off by the grid anyway, which is why no tile in any version of Xenon has had one. Tiles cast a shadow now, the slider controls it, and the global theme's shadow control finally does something too. Short screens like the Xeneon Edge still have no shadow by default, and a tile that asks for one gets it.

  • A tile can be completely transparent now

    Panel opacity stopped just short of zero and, even there, kept a faint light wash and a lit top edge, so a "transparent" card was still a pale sheet over your wallpaper. The slider goes to zero and at zero the panel is genuinely gone: only the widget's own content over your background. The border and the shadow are separate controls, so an outline with nothing inside it is still something you can build on purpose.

  • The effects no longer require you to recolour the tile first

    Opacity, corner radius, glass, border and shadow were tucked inside the "Customize" colour section, which meant wanting a transparent tile forced you to take over its whole palette. They have their own Effects tab now and apply on their own. Anything you had already set is untouched.

  • Tabs inside a tile can be reordered by dragging them, in edit mode

    A tab tile, Chat, Riproduzione and Discord sitting in one tile, for instance, kept the tabs in the order you happened to add them, and the only way to change that was to remove a tab and put it back after the others. In edit mode you now drag a tab sideways along its bar: the others make room as you move it and it stays where you drop it. The order is saved with the layout, so it survives a restart and reaches the other screens you open the dashboard on. Outside edit mode a tap on a tab still just switches tab.

  • Community media widgets can seek through the track they are showing

    The SDK's existing Media permission now includes mediaSeek: a widget sends an absolute position in seconds and Xenon moves the selected system media session there on Windows, macOS or Linux. The action uses the same guarded runner as every other widget control, clamps invalid positions, reports players with no seekable timeline honestly, and is documented alongside play/pause, previous and next. This is what lets a turntable needle, waveform or ordinary progress bar become a real scrubber instead of an animation.

  • Widgets can now show which apps are using your CPU, memory and GPU

    Suggested on Discord as a mini task manager to put in place of one of the built-in panels. It ships as a new Processi permission a community widget can ask for, rather than as a change to anyone's dashboard: one person finding a panel useless is not a reason to take it off everybody's screen, and this way you install the tile if you want it and put it where you like. A widget granted it gets a fresh reading every two seconds: one row per app with its CPU percentage, its memory, and on Windows its share of the GPU. Apps are grouped the way a task manager groups them, so twenty Chrome processes are one Chrome row, and the whole-machine totals come with it so a top-ten list never looks like it is missing something.

    If your PC has more than one graphics chip, they are all listed separately, by name. This is the difference between a number you can act on and one that starts an argument. On a machine with a dedicated card and integrated graphics, the browser can be working the integrated chip hard while the dedicated card sits at nothing, and a widget that adds the two together shows a figure belonging to neither, openly contradicting the GPU tile next to it. Measured on exactly such a PC: 14.6% on the integrated Radeon while the RTX genuinely read 0%. Xenon now reports each adapter on its own, asks Windows for its real name, and a widget can let you switch between them. Works for two cards or five, and on a normal single-GPU PC nothing changes.

    It costs nothing until you install something that uses it. There is no background collector waiting to be asked and no setting to find: Xenon starts measuring because a widget you installed holds the permission and a dashboard is open, and stops as soon as either stops being true, including when you pause that widget or switch on safe mode. When it does run it is about 55 milliseconds of work every two seconds, because it reads the raw Windows performance counters and works out the difference itself instead of asking Windows to sample them, which is roughly fifty times cheaper than the obvious way of doing it.

    Per-app GPU is Windows only. macOS does not expose it outside private system interfaces, and on Linux it only works for one graphics vendor at a time, so on those two the widget is told there is no GPU figure and hides the column rather than showing a row of zeros that would read as an idle graphics card. CPU and memory work on all three.

  • The permission dialog no longer shows some permissions by their internal name

    Asking to install a widget that wanted your peripheral battery levels showed the word "battery" on its own, with no sentence explaining what it meant, at the exact moment you are deciding whether to allow it. That, and per-app audio levels in eight of the eleven languages, now read as proper sentences everywhere.

  • Your phone or tablet can now be the second screen

    Xenon has always needed a screen you were willing to give up, a Xeneon Edge, a spare monitor, an idle tablet, and that requirement, not the features, is what kept it a niche thing. You already own a screen. Settings → Telefono → Accesso dal telefono turns on a separate, opt-in door: your PC shows a QR code, you point your phone's camera at it, and the dashboard opens in the phone's browser on the same Wi-Fi. No account, no cloud, no app to install, nothing leaves your network. Each device you add is listed by name with when it last connected, can be renamed, and can be removed on its own or all at once, and removing one hangs up on it immediately rather than waiting for it to notice.

    A paired device is your dashboard, not a view of it. Deck keys really fire on the PC, settings you change there are the settings on the PC, the Store installs, the AI answers, the app switcher switches apps, and community widgets look and behave exactly as they do on your monitor. The exceptions are short and they are all the same exception: things that put a dialog, a restart or a download in front of somebody who is not standing at the computer, Windows' UAC prompt, the updater, and the installers. Plus the pairing controls themselves, so a paired device can never enrol another one or remove the device that would kick it off. That list is written in the panel, so you know before you try.

    What you accept by pairing is worth saying out loud: a device you lose, or hand to someone, is a way into your PC until you remove it. That is what the device list and the one-tap Remove all are for. And on your home network the connection is not encrypted, so use it on a network you trust. HTTPS, working away from home, and an installable phone app are the next step and are not here yet.

  • And it can now be a proper, encrypted connection that works away from home

    The phone door above is plain HTTP on your own Wi-Fi, which is fine on a network you trust and is also why a browser withholds a whole set of things from it: a phone will not let a page install itself as an app, use the microphone, or send you notifications unless the connection is encrypted. Settings → Telefono → Accesso sicuro, anche fuori casa turns on a second door: Xenon serves the same dashboard over HTTPS on your Tailscale address, with a real certificate, and the address it gives you works from your sofa and from another country without opening a single port on your router. It also stops the address from changing: the local one is an IP your router can reassign at any time, and when it does, every device you paired looks unpaired. Nothing is replaced, the local door stays exactly as it was for anyone who does not use Tailscale, and this one has to be switched on deliberately. If it cannot come up, the panel says which of the four things is missing (Tailscale not installed, not running, not signed in, or its certificates not enabled for your network) instead of a red cross. Configura per me now handles the second of those itself, in both the shapes it comes in. Tailscale can end up installed with its background service stopped, and it can also end up with that service running while its own app is not, and on Windows the second one is enough to stop everything: Tailscale answers every question normally, reports itself as neither signed out nor connected, and stays that way forever with nothing in its logs. Xenon now starts whichever of the two is missing and carries on, so the button gets you to a working connection from either state. If it cannot, you get a sentence naming the one that is stuck and what to do about it, instead of five minutes of "waiting for you to finish signing in" for a sign-in that never opened. Devices paired on the local address need pairing once more here, because a browser ties a pairing to the address it was made on.

    And it comes back on its own after a restart. The secure door used to ask Tailscale one question a few seconds after your PC started and treat the answer as final. On Windows that is too early by design: the Tailscale service starts with the machine, its app starts with your session, and until that app has caught up Tailscale says it has no connection yet. So after every reboot the door stayed down, and the panel kept repeating the reason from that first moment long after Tailscale had connected, which made it look as though Xenon could not see it. The only way out was pressing Configura per me again, and because the door was down, the phone fell back to the local address and asked to be paired again. Xenon now keeps asking until the door is up, backing off to a check every few minutes, and the panel shows the reason as it is now rather than the one from startup. Reported on Discord by Wayfinder, on Windows 11 with an Android phone.

  • And it can tell you something happened while the app is closed

    A countdown you set on the dashboard was only useful while you were looking at the dashboard, which is a strange thing for a timer to be. With the secure connection on, Settings → Telefono → Notifiche lets each device switch notifications on for itself, and a timer that runs out reaches the phone in your pocket. It is off until you turn it on, once per device, and there is a Provala button so you can find out it works now instead of at three in the morning. This is also the one thing in Xenon that goes out to somebody else, so it says so plainly on the switch: notifications physically cannot work without your phone's own push service (Apple, Google or Mozilla), that single shared connection is why they cost no battery, and the text is encrypted end to end, so what passes through them is bytes they cannot read. No account, no server of ours in the middle: your PC talks to the push service directly. Nothing else notifies you, by design, no digests, no "come back" nudges, and nothing from your calendar or your notes: a lock screen is a public surface.

  • The dashboard now fits the screen it is on, including a tablet

    Xenon stacked its tiles into one column on a phone and drew the full 24-column grid everywhere else, with nothing in between, so a tablet got the desktop layout at a third of the width. On a 768px iPad that is a 32px column, which makes an ordinary tile 256px of squeezed widget, and it measured worse than the phone did: 30 pieces of content cut off by their own container against 9 at phone size. Tablets now stack in two columns, keeping their reading order, with the ordinary topbar rather than the phone's compact one. As before, nothing about your saved layout is touched, this is only how it is drawn on that screen, and the same dashboard opened on your PC is unchanged. A display mounted vertically, like a Xeneon Edge stood on its end, is deliberately left on the grid: it is tall, not small, and somebody built that layout for exactly that shape.

  • Stacked tiles now follow the order you actually see

    Tiles were ordered by their grid row, and a tile nudged two rows down, about 70px, which nobody reads as a new row, counted as a whole line of its own. Three tiles side by side came out left, right, middle. They are grouped into visual rows first now, so a row reads left to right whatever its tiles' exact rows are.

  • Things that were being cut off on a small screen are not any more

    The Settings window laid its category list and its footer side by side below a certain width, which made the window wider than the phone it was on: about 150px of every panel was simply gone, and the close button sat off the right edge where it could not be tapped. The window fits now, and on a phone the category list became a picker instead of a wall of chips (below). The top bar was sharing its shortfall out among everything in it rather than dropping anything, so two buttons were sliced down the middle, the clock lost its leading digit and two status chips were squeezed to a sliver of a letter each, controls keep their size now, and what does not fit is left out instead. The System widget's cards were clipping their own second line, so RAM showed its percentage and half of "DDR5 6000 MHz" and the disk card half of its file system; the cards take the height their text needs and the panel scrolls. The calendar was losing a few pixels off every row to a grid column that had never been told to stay inside its tile.

  • Music no longer empties the top bar on a phone

    With "music takes over the island" on, a playing track masked every other segment to give the player the whole capsule, including on a phone, where the player is not shown at all because it does not fit beside a clock at 390px. The result was a bar with the time, the date and the weather all gone for as long as something was playing. The takeover now applies only where the player it is making room for is actually on screen.

  • With that on, Xenon installs onto the phone as an app

    Once the connection is encrypted the phone stops treating the dashboard as a web page it happens to be showing: Add to Home Screen gives it its own icon, and tapping that opens Xenon full screen with no address bar and no browser tabs above it. The microphone starts working too, Xenon AI by voice, using the phone's own microphone rather than the PC's, which is what it had been falling back to. And when the PC is off, opening the app shows Xenon's own screen saying it cannot reach it, instead of the browser's error page. It is not an offline dashboard and cannot be: everything on it comes from a computer that is not on. Nothing is cached while your PC is reachable, so an update to Xenon arrives on the next open exactly as it always has.

  • And on a phone, the dashboard is finally shaped like a phone

    Reaching Xenon from a phone would not have been worth much if what arrived was the desktop layout at one-sixth scale, which is exactly what it was: the dashboard is a 24-column grid, and on a 390px screen that is a 16px column, so a carefully built layout rendered as a perfect, unreadable miniature of itself. On a phone screen the tiles now stack into one column, in the same order you read them on your PC, left to right, top to bottom, each keeping the height you gave it, so a tile you made twice as tall is still twice as tall. Turning the phone on its side keeps the stacked view: a phone lying down is still a phone, and the width it gains it pays for in height, which is what was clipping every tile halfway through. Your layout is not touched, moved or re-saved: this is only how it is *drawn* on a small screen, and the same dashboard opened on your PC a second later is exactly as you left it. The top bar folds into one compact row, the clock stops competing with the one your phone already shows, and the controls you actually press, search, Xenon AI, apps, settings, and moving between pages, sit in a bar at the bottom of the screen, where a thumb can reach them. Notches and home indicators are respected. Layout editing is hidden here, because dragging tiles around a grid you are not being shown at its real size is a good way to lose one. A tablet keeps the full grid, which is the point of a tablet, an iPad held either way is well above the threshold, so what you get there is your dashboard as you built it. If you would rather have one and are given the other (a small window, a phone you want the grid on anyway), the choice is yours and it is remembered on that device only, it never travels to your PC.

  • You can now try Xenon in your browser, without installing anything

    Every link to Xenon used to end at a download button, which is a lot to ask of someone who has never seen the thing. xenon-app.com/demo is the real dashboard, the same code, every widget, the layout editor, the themes, the Store, running on simulated data. The CPU load moves, the temperatures lag behind it the way real ones do, the music plays and changes track, and pressing pause actually pauses it. Nothing on the page can touch a computer: anything that would run something on a PC answers "this one runs on your PC" instead, and the handful of tiles that only exist because they stream from a real machine say so on their face. Your changes are yours and stay in your browser. It works in all 11 of the app's languages and follows the one you were reading the site in.

  • Every theme, background and page in the catalog now has a "Try in your browser" button

    Until now a catalog entry gave you a code to copy and paste into an app you had to install first, which meant the catalog was really only useful to people who already had Xenon. Those entries now open straight in the demo with the creation loaded into the app's own import dialog, the same preview you would get on your own machine, so you see exactly what it contains before it applies. Deck profiles, widgets, scenes and packs do not get the button: they genuinely need a PC, and a button that leads to a failure is worse than no button.

  • Share your setup as a picture, the share card is back, and it finally photographs the right screen

    Xenon had a share card once, and it was removed in v4.5.2 for one reason: the "real screenshot" behind it grabbed the entire desktop, and on a multi-monitor PC it usually grabbed the wrong monitor. That is fixed, and the fix is the whole point. Xenon no longer works out a rectangle to photograph, it works out *which display* your dashboard is on, by its shape, and asks for exactly that one. Shapes survive Windows' display scaling where pixel coordinates do not, which is what made the old version guess wrong. And when it cannot be certain, two identically shaped monitors, the dashboard inside iCUE, Edge preview switched on, a game running full screen, it does not guess: it draws the card instead, and tells you in a line under the preview why. The screenshot is now the subject rather than a dimmed backdrop: your dashboard sits in a framed plate with your palette, the name, and a QR code that leads whoever sees the picture to the creation or to Xenon itself. Two shapes, Post 16:9 for Reddit and Discord and Story 9:16 for TikTok and Shorts, so neither platform crops your card for you. You always see the finished image before anything leaves the app, and you can download it, copy it straight to the clipboard, or hand it to the system share sheet. Find it in Settings → Condividi & Importa → 📸 Condividi il mio setup, or on any share dialog when you export a theme, a page or a Deck profile.

  • What is on screen when you share it stays yours

    A dashboard casually shows a lot about you: calendar entries with their locations, your notes, your task list, your Discord name, file search results with full paths, whatever Claude Code is doing. Posting that publicly is the kind of thing you do once and regret. So Blur personal details is on the first time, and it blurs those widgets, notes, tasks, calendar, agenda, chat, Claude, Discord, notifications, search and cameras, in the image only, never on your screen. You can switch it off per card if there is nothing sensitive up, and Xenon remembers your choice.

  • Announcements can show a picture or a short clip

    An announcement was a title and two lines of text, so a release worth *looking* at had to be described in prose instead. A card can now carry one image, GIF or clip above the text: a clip plays muted and on a loop with no controls, like a GIF at a fraction of the weight, and it stays on its first frame if your system asks for reduced motion. The file comes from Xenon's own asset host and nowhere else, so an announcement can never pull an image from a stranger's server. It appears on a full card only, a corner toast has no room for one. Nothing about this changes what the channel knows about you: the same list still reaches every install, your dashboard still decides on your own PC which messages apply to it, and announcements can still be switched off for good from the card itself or from Settings.

  • A widget can now fill the screen when you tap it

    Some things do not fit in a tile. A board, a map, a game: they were being designed around a small rectangle, or split into a tile plus a separate fullscreen Ambient scene just to have room. A widget can now ask to cover the whole dashboard, and go back to being a tile when you are done. It only ever happens because you touched the widget: a widget cannot take the screen while you are reading something else, cannot do it from the background, and cannot do it while you are rearranging your layout. The way out is Xenon's, not the widget's, so it is always the same and always there: the ✕ in the top right corner, the Escape key, or simply swiping to another dashboard page. The widget is not restarted on the way in or on the way out, so a game keeps its game and a map keeps its position. Creators ask for it with "expand": true, and you approve it like any other permission, described in plain words: "It can fill the screen (when you tap it)".

  • The Store's front page can be arranged, and it now has an Archive

    Limited drops, supporter-only packs and free creations all landed in the same spotlight with the same visual weight, in an order that was written into the code, so nothing could be moved without shipping a new version. The order of the sections, whether each one is shown at all, and the shape it draws in (a scrolling row, a grid, a big lead card) are now settings, kept with the catalog itself. Both Stores read the same arrangement, the one inside Xenon and the one on the website, so they can no longer show you different things. Two new sections come with it: Just added, the most recent free creations, and an Archive at the bottom holding drops whose copies are all gone, quiet and out of the way but still there to look at and search. Sold-out drops move there instead of sitting next to something you can still claim. Two shelves are deliberately outside all of this and cannot be hidden by any arrangement: updates for things you already installed, and what is new since your last visit. Those describe your dashboard, not a shop window.

  • The Archive was never showing anything, and it does now

    A drop whose copies were all gone was being dropped from the page before the Archive could receive it, so the section it was built for stayed permanently empty while any other drop was still claimable. NØVA // NEON DISTRICT is in there now, which is where a finished drop belongs.

  • The Supporters and Limited sections are real carousels now, with arrows and no scrollbar

    They were meant to be a single swipeable row and had never been one: a CSS rule declared later in the file quietly won, so each of them stayed a stack of full-width cards, one under another, eating a screen apiece. Making them rows then exposed the next problem, which had been there all along and hidden by the first: the row could not be moved by anything except a finger. The slow auto-advance had never once animated, and arrows would not have worked either. Both were asking the browser for a smooth scroll that the browser simply dropped. So the row no longer scrolls at all: it slides, which is something a page can actually do. You get the classic arrows on the left and right, each one fading out when there is nothing further that way, the last card lands flush against the right edge instead of stopping short, dragging with a finger or the mouse still works and lands on a card rather than half of one, and the pale system scrollbar under the black page is gone because there is nothing left to scroll. The auto-advance works for the first time, and it stops for good the moment you move the row yourself. A section holding a single drop still spans the full width instead of sitting in a lonely fixed-width track. And each of the three exclusive sections can be drawn either as those large cards or as the compact grid the rest of the catalog uses, which is roughly a third of the height for the same content.

  • What supporting actually gets you is now the first thing on the catalog page

    The panel explaining the tier (the perks, how long access lasts, how your personal code reaches you) sat halfway down the page, above the supporter drops. That is the wrong way round: you met a locked card long before you met the explanation of what a locked card is. The panel now leads the page, unchanged, and the supporter drops keep their own place further down under a plain heading. Turning the Supporters section off in the arrangement still removes both halves together.

  • A limited drop can no longer be missing from the home page

    The home page picks the two creations to show from what is marked as featured, which is right, except that copies of a limited drop run out while everything else stays available forever. When both featured entries happened to be supporter packs, the one time-critical thing on the site was the one thing not on it. The lead card is still whatever was chosen; the second place now goes to a live limited drop whenever there is one.

  • The support address in the app, on the site and in the changelog is the working one

    It pointed at an old personal mailbox that is no longer where supporter mail is read. Everywhere it appears it now reads support@xenon-app.com, which is the address your code email already comes from.

  • The YouTube widget plays YouTube now

    It was built entirely around going live: viewer count, stream health, a Go live button. If you never stream, the whole tile added up to a card saying "Offline". It is now a real player as well. There is a video player in the tile, and under it your own library to browse: Liked, Playlists, Subscriptions (the newest uploads from the channels you follow) and Search. Tap a video and it plays right there on the Xeneon Edge, with play/pause, previous/next, a progress bar you can drag, mute, and a button that blows the player up to the full screen. The rest of the list becomes the queue, so it moves on to the next video by itself. The widget arranges itself around the tile you give it: on a wide short tile, the shape the Xeneon Edge encourages, the list moves next to the video instead of under it, which is worth several times the picture size. On a tall tile it stays stacked, because there the video is already using the full width. Either way the list stays reachable, and a tile too small for both scrolls instead of hiding what is at the bottom. Everything reads from the account you already connected, nothing new to set up and no new permissions, because the connection you made for streaming already covered reading your own library. A video whose uploader has disabled embedding says so and offers to open in your browser instead. Player and library are separate cards you can reorder or switch off. Broadcasting is not in this widget at all any more, it has its own (below). This started the day after a user told us he had set the widget up expecting exactly this; thanks, Jotun.

  • Streaming to YouTube is its own widget now, and it can actually start a stream

    Watching YouTube and broadcasting on YouTube were sharing one tile, which meant a viewer got half a dashboard of controls they would never press and a streamer got a video player in the way. They are two widgets now: YouTube to watch, YouTube Live to broadcast. Both read the same connected account, so there is nothing extra to set up. The streaming one is also worth having, which is the real change. It could previously only flip a live that you had already created in YouTube Studio, so the button spent most of its life unable to do anything. Now it creates one: give it a title, choose who can watch, press the button, and Xenon makes the broadcast and sets up your channel's streaming endpoint if you have never streamed before. It goes on air by itself the moment OBS starts sending, so there is no moment where you press a button and are told the encoder is not ready. There is the live chat, read and write, right on the touchscreen next to the game. And the small things you keep a browser tab open for: who can watch, switched while you are live; the link to the stream, copied in one tap; and your stream key for OBS, hidden behind a Show button and readable only on the PC itself, never from a paired phone, because whoever has it can broadcast to your channel. Chat is the one part that costs YouTube quota while it runs, so it only reads while you are actually live and its card is on screen, at the pace YouTube itself asks for.

  • Twitch has a watching widget too, separate from the streaming one

    The Twitch tile was the streamer's side of Twitch: go live, clip, marker, ad, chat modes. If you watch Twitch rather than stream on it, none of that was for you. There is now a second widget, called simply Twitch, and it is a player: pick a channel and the stream runs in the tile. Three lists to pick from, Followed (the channels you follow that are on air right now, with how many people are watching each), Top (the busiest channels on Twitch at this moment) and Search. There is a full screen button that fills the Xeneon Edge, with the controls fading out a few seconds in and coming back at a touch, and an optional chat card that shows the chat of whatever you are watching, off until you switch it on. The chat is read anonymously and drawn by Xenon, not Twitch's embed: the embed is a whole twitch.tv page, so it arrived with Twitch's cookie and advertising panel across it and then spent its height on a header, an event banner, a message box and a footer, leaving about two lines for the conversation. Reading a channel's chat needs no account, so the messages come over the same anonymous connection the streamer's Twitch tile has used for versions. No cookie panel, no third-party page, every pixel of the card is chat, and it looks like the rest of the dashboard. You can write in it too, sent with your own connected account, so the box works on the touchscreen whether or not the browser showing the dashboard is signed in to Twitch. When a channel refuses a message because it is followers only, subscribers only or in slow mode, it says so instead of swallowing it. Emotes are drawn as emotes, both the ones arriving in the chat and the ones you send: there is a picker next to the box holding the channel's own emotes and the global ones, and tapping one drops its code in the message. The streamer's Twitch tile shows emotes in its chat now too, since both read through the same code. The one thing left that only the Twitch page has is channel points and the paid chat extras, and there is a button beside the box that opens the real chat for those. The streamer's tile is untouched and is now called Twitch Live so the two are easy to tell apart. Both read the same connected account. Play, pause, volume and quality stay in Twitch's own player where they already were, so there are no duplicate controls doing the same job. One thing worth knowing: Followed needs a permission the old connection did not ask for, so if you connected Twitch before this version the Followed list will ask you to reconnect once in Settings. It says exactly that instead of failing, and Top and Search work either way.

  • Community widgets can use Twitch and YouTube now

    Everything the two new tiles learned to read stayed locked inside them, which meant a widget could start your stream and had no way of knowing whether you were live. Three things a widget can now ask permission for: who you follow is live right now, with the title, the game and the viewer count, plus which channel your Twitch tile is playing; the chat of the channel you are watching, handed over already split into text and emotes so the widget can draw it in its own style instead of parsing Twitch's format; and your own YouTube broadcast, with live state, viewers, likes and stream health. There is also one new thing a widget can do: play a channel or a video in the Twitch and YouTube tiles you already have, so someone can build the "my streamers" panel they want, with the faces and the layout they want, and a tap plays it on the Edge. Each of these is a separate permission shown by name in the install dialog, and all of them are off until you approve them. What none of them costs is a second connection: a widget gets a copy of what the builtin tile has already read, so a dashboard with the tile on it pays nothing extra, and the chat is never opened just because a widget asked for it. And none of them can write. No sending a message in someone's chat, no starting or configuring a broadcast, no stream key. Publishing text in public under your name needs your own tap in the tile that owns it. The developer documentation was updated in the same change, including the part that is generated from the code so it cannot drift from what is actually allowed.

  • Linux has in-game FPS, game mode and a global search shortcut

    Three of the remaining gaps on Linux are closed, each with the platform's own answer rather than a stub. FPS come from MangoHud: install it from your package manager and launch a game with it (mangohud %command% as a Steam launch option) and the number appears on the system tile and in the Game Companion, Xenon sets MangoHud's logging up for you. It only works for games launched that way, and that is not a shortcut taken: Linux exposes no per-process frame counter at all, so a game's frame rate cannot be read without the game's own cooperation, and inventing one would have been worse than saying so. Game mode works now too, having been inert on Linux since the port: the focused window is read from the window manager's own properties, which keeps working on a Wayland session for X11 and Proton games, and on sway and Hyprland through their own IPC, so ambient effects pause when you play, Performance Mode knows what you are doing, and the screen-time breakdown fills in. When the focused window is a native Wayland one Xenon says it cannot see it instead of reusing the last one it could, because a stale reading would leave game mode stuck on after you quit. And the global search shortcut is registered as a real GNOME custom shortcut, visible, editable and deletable in your own Keyboard settings under the name "Xenon Search", and reported as taken rather than silently overwritten if something else already owns the combination.

  • The now-playing tile works on Linux with nothing installed

    It used to need playerctl, and without that package the tile simply stayed empty, on a desktop that was publishing the track on D-Bus the whole time. Xenon now reads that bus itself through busctl, which ships with systemd, the same systemd it already uses to start at login. Title, artist, album, cover art, progress and the previous/play-pause/next buttons all work out of the box. If playerctl does happen to be installed it is still preferred, because it pushes changes instead of being polled, so the tile updates the instant the track does.

  • The Linux app switcher no longer asks you to install anything to see your windows

    Listing the open windows needed wmctrl; it now needs only xprop, which comes with the X11 tools any graphical session already has. wmctrl is still what lets the tile *focus* or *close* a window, which is the part that genuinely needs it, and the buttons say so rather than failing quietly.

  • Settings no longer offers Mac and Linux features that cannot exist there

    Second screen and the Sunshine half of Remote Control rendered in full on both, and every button in them led to a failure, Second screen needs a Windows display driver, and Sunshine installs as a Windows service through winget. Both panels are now hidden outside Windows, which is what the rest of Xenon already does with anything unavailable.
