The second screen is also gone from the widget palette on those platforms, and a tile that was added on a Windows machine and opened on a Mac now says the feature is Windows-only rather than telling a Mac to install the Microsoft Store's App Installer. The game-mode panel stopped offering the PresentMon download on Linux too, and explains MangoHud instead.

  • The secure connection from outside the house works on Mac and Linux too

    This was very nearly cut for being "the Windows part", and that turned out to be one line of code rather than a fact: the Tailscale CLI, the certificate it holds, and the TLS listener Xenon puts on top of them are identical on all three systems, and the only thing tying any of it to Windows was a hardcoded C:\Program Files path. So the encrypted door, the address that works from another country, the installable phone app and the push notifications are all available on macOS and Linux now, the same panel, the same setup button, the same four reasons when something is missing. One step is yours instead of ours: Xenon installs Tailscale for you only on Windows, through winget, and driving Homebrew or apt under sudo from a switch in a dashboard is not something it should do behind your back. So on a Mac or a Linux box you install Tailscale once yourself and Xenon does everything after it. If it is not there the panel says so and prints the exact command for your system, instead of offering a button that could only ever fail. Linux has one more of these: tailscale will not take orders from your user account until it is told to, so if that is what is in the way the panel names it and prints sudo tailscale set --operator=$USER, rather than reporting it as "the service is not running" and sending you to restart something that never stopped. Pairing a phone or tablet on your own Wi-Fi never needed any of this and has worked everywhere all along: it is plain HTTP and a QR code.

  • Xenon runs on macOS

    This is the first step and it is honest about what it covers: the backend starts on a Mac and the dashboard, the widget Store, every data widget, the cloud AI, network lighting, the streaming integrations, Spotify and Wave Link work there the way they do on Windows. The parts that read the machine itself have been rewritten for macOS rather than left broken: disks, network traffic, open applications, system volume and the microphone all come from native tools, and Xenon speaks and plays its sounds through the Mac's own audio. Temperatures and GPU load no longer need anything installed: the Xenon companion reads the thermal sensors and the graphics load straight from the Mac, without ever asking for an administrator password. Where it cannot read them it falls back to macmon if you have it, and shows "--" when neither is available, which is what it always did. Things that exist only on Windows (hotkeys and text injection, per-app volume, the Store-app launcher) no longer appear as Deck keys on a Mac instead of being offered and then failing. Windows is untouched by all of this.

  • On a Mac, Xenon can now see the folders macOS protects

    The Trash and much of your cache folder are behind a permission that macOS grants per app, and the way the backend used to start meant that permission would have had to be given to Node itself, which would have handed it to every unrelated script on your machine. The Xenon app now starts the backend itself, so one grant to Xenon covers it, shown in System Settings under a name you recognise and revocable at any time. The difference is not small: on the machine this was measured on, the Trash alone was 2.4 GB the cleanup could not see, and the disk map was under-reporting by 15 GB. Grant it from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access, add Xenon, then quit and reopen it; without it nothing breaks, those folders simply stay out of the map. One thing to know until Xenon is signed by an Apple developer certificate: macOS ties that permission to the app's signature, and an unsigned build gets a new one at every release, so you have to grant it again after each update, by toggling Xenon off and on in that list (or removing it and adding it back). The sign that it has lapsed is a Trash that reads 0 B, or the disk map suddenly accounting for several GB less than before.

  • Search and the Disk widget work on Mac and Linux

    Both are built on the living file index, and on those platforms the index could never start: the folder you pointed it at was rewritten into a Windows-style path and then rejected as invalid, so it held nothing, and there was no value you could type to fix it. Searching therefore found nothing and blamed Windows Search for it, on a Mac, while the Disk widget failed to open at all. The index now accepts the folders those systems actually have, starts on your home folder out of the box, and the companion answers it in the shape the dashboard reads, so results, the folder map, the biggest-files list, the duplicate finder and the cleanup categories all work. When no folder is set the search box now says which setting turns it on instead of naming a Windows component.

  • The memory reading on Mac and Linux is the real one

    It used to sit at 99% and stay there on any Mac, because the figure Xenon asks the system for means "completely unused" there and "free for a new program to take" on Windows, and macOS and Linux both keep the first number near zero on purpose, by using spare memory for caching. Each platform is now asked its own version of the right question: on a Mac the number matches the one Activity Monitor shows you, and on Linux it matches what the kernel reports as available.

  • The Mac app switcher is instant, and asks for no permission

    The list of open applications is read from the Mac's own window server rather than by scripting each app in turn, which takes milliseconds instead of seconds and, more importantly, needs no Automation permission, macOS prompts once per application for that, and a single "Don't Allow" used to leave the tile permanently empty with nothing inside Xenon to undo it. Focusing and quitting an app go the same way. Where the companion is not installed the old path still answers, exactly as before.

  • Cleaning up disk space works on Mac and Linux

    The Disk widget's categories, the drill-down into a folder and the Clean button all behave there the way they do on Windows: deleted items go to the Trash so anything can be put back, the same protected places are refused, and a folder held open by a running program gives up everything around the locked file instead of refusing as a whole. On a Mac the temp files category in particular could be listed but never actually cleaned.

  • The media tile knows what your Mac is playing

    Whatever is playing (Music, Spotify, a video in Safari or Chrome, a podcast) shows up with its title, artist, album and cover art, the progress moves as the track does, and the previous, play/pause and next buttons work, on the tile, in the top bar and as Deck keys. This is the same media panel Windows has, reading the Mac instead of a Windows session, so nothing about how it looks or behaves is different. macOS keeps now-playing behind an interface that only Apple-signed programs may open, so Xenon uses the standard bridge for it, which the installer fetches and puts in place for you. If it is not there, the tile says nothing is playing and the media Deck keys are not offered, rather than being offered and doing nothing.

  • The Mac version installs and updates itself like the Windows one

    There is now a Xenon app for macOS, built as a universal binary so it runs natively on both Apple Silicon and Intel. Opening it on a Mac that has no dashboard behind it offers to set one up, in a Terminal window you can read and stop, and the download is checked against the release signature before a single file is extracted. Once installed it starts again at every login and keeps itself running. Updates work the same way they do on Windows: the new version is downloaded and verified first, and only then swapped in, with the previous version restored if the new one fails to start. Local voice also works, using the Whisper build Homebrew ships, which runs on the Mac's GPU. Until an Apple developer certificate is in place macOS will ask you to confirm the app the first time you open it.

  • Linux catches up on the things that were missing

    The media tile now shows what is playing and its buttons work, reading the standard the Linux desktop already publishes, so Spotify, your browser, VLC and the rest all appear without any per-app setup. Talking to Xenon works too: the microphone opens for voice commands and for the "Hey Xenon" wake word, and the assistant can see your screen on X11. Graphics cards other than NVIDIA finally report themselves, with AMD giving load, temperature and memory straight from the kernel and needing nothing installed at all, and Intel giving its temperature. Your desktop notifications can be mirrored to the dashboard the way Windows ones are, with the same rules: they are only read while a dashboard is open, they are never written to disk and they never leave your machine. The embedded browser tile works on both Mac and Linux now, using whichever Chromium-based browser you have. And there is a Fedora package alongside the AppImage and the .deb.

  • Linux can now install and update Xenon, not just run it

    The Linux tiles have worked since v4.7, but there was no way to set the thing up: you started the server by hand every time and updates meant downloading and replacing the folder yourself. The same installer that handles macOS now handles Linux too. It registers a service that starts Xenon when you log in and brings it back if it crashes, and it tells you which optional tools are missing and what each one would light up rather than failing silently later. In-app updates work as well, with the same care taken on Windows: the new version is verified before anything is extracted, and if it does not start, the previous one is put back exactly as it was. On a desktop without systemd it falls back to a normal autostart entry and says so, including that the fallback has no crash-restart. Uninstalling is one command and leaves your settings alone unless you ask for them to go too.

  • Linux has a Xenon app too, not just the browser

    There is now an AppImage and a .deb of the full-screen Xenon window, the same one Windows and macOS have. Open it once and, if there is no dashboard behind it yet, it offers to set one up in a terminal window you can read and stop, checking the download against the release signature before anything is extracted. After that it starts the dashboard for you if the service is not running, and it updates itself the way the other two do. The install is per user on purpose, so the .deb does not do it for you at install time: everything it would create (where the dashboard lives, your settings, the service that starts it at login) belongs to one account, and a package installs as root for the whole machine. The first launch is the moment that knows whose Xenon this is. If your desktop has no terminal program at all the app cannot show you the installer, and the README's manual command is the way in.

  • The download now has an installer for your system, in plain sight

    Extracting the source zip showed exactly one thing you could open, INSTALL.bat, so on a Mac or on Linux the reasonable conclusion was that there was nothing there for you, and the installer that did exist sat two folders down where you had no reason to look. The folder now carries all three side by side: INSTALL.bat on Windows, INSTALL.command on macOS (Finder runs it on a double-click), INSTALL.sh on Linux, each with its uninstaller beside it. They do the same thing and always did; only the extension your system is willing to launch is different.

  • The lock key locks your Mac again, and re-running the installer now updates the companion

    The Deck's "lock the PC" key called a small system program that Apple has since removed from macOS, so on a current Mac it did nothing at all, and did it silently, because a key that fails looks exactly like a key nobody pressed. It now asks macOS to lock the way the Lock Screen menu item does, immediately, whatever your password settings say. Underneath that is a second fix with a longer reach: the installer used to skip the Xenon companion whenever one was already present, so a Mac stayed on whichever version it first downloaded forever and never saw anything added later. It now checks the version and replaces an older one, which is how this fix, and every future companion feature, actually reaches machines that are already set up. A failed download can no longer leave you without a working companion either.

  • The notifications tile says what it can do on your system, instead of loading forever

    On anything that is not Windows the tile sat on "Connecting…" and stayed there, because the part that reads your notifications simply is not there and nothing ever said so. On a Mac it now tells you the feature is not available on this system, which is the truth and takes a second to read, rather than looking like something that is about to finish and never does. The same message covers any other system without support, and on Windows nothing changes. This also fixes the Linux mirroring described above actually switching on: it was written but never started, so on Linux the tile showed the same endless loading even though the feature was there.

  • When someone calls you, the dashboard rings

    Discord, Teams, Zoom, the phone on your desk through Phone Link: when a call comes in, Xenon takes the screen with a card that shows who is calling, and three buttons, Rispondi, Rifiuta, Silenzia. It rings on the Xeneon Edge, in the app, in a browser, and on a paired phone, and answering on one closes the card on all of them. If your phone is locked and paired, it gets a push, so the call reaches you even with the screen off. Turn it on in Settings → Notifiche → Chiamate in arrivo. What the button does depends on the app, and Xenon only shows the buttons that are real on your machine rather than a hopeful Rispondi that does nothing. Discord is the one it answers properly: connecting your Discord account lets Xenon join the call outright, on Windows, macOS and Linux alike, with no window jumping to the front. Teams and Zoom are answered the way you would by hand: Xenon brings their window forward and presses the shortcut they document. That works on Windows today, on a Mac once you allow Xenon Helper under Accessibility, and on Linux where xdotool or ydotool is installed. Where nothing can pick up, a mirrored phone call, WhatsApp, Slack, the card still rings and offers to open the app, and says so in one line instead of leaving a gap where a button should be. The card goes away when the call does. A ringing notification is temporary, on a phone call mirrored from your phone it is there while it rings and gone the instant you hang up, with nothing posted in its place, so Xenon watches for it disappearing rather than waiting out a timer. Hang up, decline on your phone, or let it stop ringing, and the card closes within a couple of seconds. If the call ends in a way that leaves nothing behind at all, it still closes itself once a real ring would have finished, and you can always dismiss it by hand. Two things worth knowing before you rely on it. The audio stays on the PC: answering from your phone means the PC picks up, which is useful when you are wearing your headset and mid-game, and not useful when you are in another room. And outside Discord there is no way to ask Windows or Linux whether a notification is a call, so Xenon reads the wording of it. That works across all eleven languages Xenon speaks and deliberately ignores anything that reads as a missed or ended call, but it can miss one, and Settings lets you switch off any app you would rather never rang. Discord is the exception and the best case, but it has its own edge: Xenon learns about a Discord call from the notification Discord itself raises, so if you are already looking at Discord when the call comes in, Discord shows no notification and Xenon shows no card, you can see the call anyway.

  • The Deck's keyboard-shortcut key works on macOS and Linux

    It was written for Windows and quietly stayed there: the key existed in the editor on every system, and on a Mac or a Linux machine it simply failed. It now sends the combination on macOS through Xenon Helper (allow it once under Accessibility) and on Linux through xdotool or ydotool. Where none of those is available the key no longer appears in the editor at all, instead of being offered and then failing.

  • The Calcio tile is about the football now, not about the list of teams you follow

    It used to draw one row per followed team with that team's entire existence squeezed into a two line cell on the right, and a search box pinned across the top for an action most people do four times ever. Worse, everything on it came from a single fixture: if the provider had no match for your club in its window, which is most of July, the row had nothing at all in it, not even the crest, because the crest was being read off the match. Four teams, four crest placeholders, four times "Nessuna partita". It now leads with the one match that matters right now, across everything you follow: the game in play if there is one, otherwise the next kickoff, otherwise the last result. Both crests, the score or the kickoff time, the competition and the ground, tinted with the home club's own colours. Under it, three tabs. Partite merges every followed team's and competition's fixtures into one list grouped by day, Oggi and Domani first and results underneath, so a derby between two of your clubs is one row rather than the same match printed twice. Classifica was buried inside a team's detail view and is now a tab of its own, with a chip for each competition you follow and the last five results of every side. It also says something it used to leave you to work out: without the optional TheSportsDB Premium key the data source hands back only the top five places, for any league, so the tab prints that under the table instead of showing five rows as though they were the whole thing. Notizie is new: headlines about your clubs in your own language, using the same feed reader the News tile already uses, fetched only when you open the tab. Crests now arrive whether or not there is a match. Xenon fetches each club's identity once and keeps it for a day: crest, colours, ground, capacity and the year it was founded. That is also what a club's page shows when the calendar is empty, so an out of season tile shows you your clubs instead of an empty list. Adding a team moved into a + next to the tabs, which is also where you remove one. All of it works on a phone and on the Xeneon Edge: the tile drops the hero on a short layout and the form column on a narrow one, rather than clipping. Live minute by minute scores still need the optional TheSportsDB Premium key, as before; without it you get the kickoff time and then the final score.

  • A widget can now turn one person in a Discord call up or down

    Changing how loud somebody is in a voice channel means finding them in Discord and right-clicking, which means leaving whatever you were doing. A community widget can now show the people in your channel with a volume slider and a mute for each one, and Xenon applies it without Discord ever coming to the front. It only changes what you hear: nobody else in the call is affected, nothing about it is visible to them, and it has nothing to do with server moderation, so it works in a channel where you are just another member. The same thing works the other way as well: Xenon now reports how loud each person currently is, so a slider opens where you actually left it rather than in the middle. Your own row is not one of these controls, because Discord has no such setting for yourself; your microphone and output levels are the separate keys they always were. Nothing needs reconnecting, the permission is the Discord one you have already granted the widget, and a volume you set holds for as long as Discord and Xenon are both open. Close Discord and everyone goes back to normal, which is Discord's own behaviour and not something Xenon can keep. Asked for by Swiv on the Xenon forum, and documented in the Widget SDK.

Changes

  • The anonymous install counter now says a little more about the install, and still nothing about you

    If you have the counter switched on in Settings → Generale → Aggiornamenti, its once-a-day note used to carry two things: your version and your operating system. It now also carries how old this install is as one of five ranges, the month it first ran, the version it came from on the first ping after an update, whether this is its first start of the week and of the month, and your interface language. That is the whole list, and the settings panel links straight to the page that spells it out. There is still no identifier of any kind, still no extra network request, it rides the update check that already runs, and still nothing about what you actually do with the dashboard: not which widgets you use, not what you search for, not what you open.

    Why it changed. With only a version number I could see that some installs were on an old release and had no way to tell whether those people had upgraded or simply stopped using Xenon, and no way at all to know how many installs were being used in a given week. Those are the two questions that decide what gets built next, and guessing at them badly is worse than not asking. The awkward part is that "how many *different* installs this week" normally needs an identifier, so the server can tell two visits from one PC apart from two PCs. It does not have one here: your own PC remembers the last week it reported and simply says "first time this week", once. The server adds 1 and learns nothing else.

    On my side it is stored in pieces, deliberately. Each of those fields is counted in its own table, never together in one row, because a single row holding version *and* system *and* age *and* birth month *and* language could describe one particular person, and since most of that barely changes from day to day, consecutive days could be stitched into one machine's history. That would be an identifier assembled from the data after going to the trouble of never sending one. Counting each field separately means the combination does not exist in the database at all. Everything is deleted after 400 days. The privacy page has the complete payload, the reasoning, and the one honest caveat: an install that already existed before this release reports its age and birth month as unknown, forever, because Xenon never recorded when it first ran and a visible gap beats a guessed number.

    Nothing switched itself on. If the counter was off it is still off; if it was on it is still on. The switch is in the same place and turning it off takes effect immediately.

  • Timers now have a stop button, so you can keep one for later

    Until now the only way to put a timer aside was to leave it paused part-way through, because the other button restarts it and immediately starts counting again. So a 20-minute timer you had used once sat on the dashboard reading 7:41 forever. Stop puts it back to its full time and holds it there, ready for the next time you need it. It appears only when it would do something: not on a timer that has finished, and not on one already sitting at its full time.

  • The graphs are drawn as curves now, not zig-zags

    Every chart in Xenon joined its readings with straight lines, which on data that jumps around (a ping that flips between two values, a CPU that idles and then spikes) came out as a row of sharp spikes with hard corners. The little graphs on the System cards and the ones in the Storico tab are now drawn as smooth curves instead. The readings themselves have not changed and neither has the scale: the curve is built so that it cannot bulge past the values it passes through, so a peak on the chart is still the peak that was measured, and a chart that prints "picco 96%" next to it is not drawing 103%. Flat stretches stay flat rather than gaining a wobble.

    And the Storico charts lost the shading behind the line. Each of those charts drew a second, faint shape above its line, between the average and the peak of each hour. It carried real information and it did not look like information: it read as a smudge sitting behind the graph, on every card, all the time. In its place the line now has a soft fade underneath it that falls away to nothing, so the card has some weight without anything competing with the line. The peak has not gone anywhere, it is the number next to each title. With the shading gone the charts also use their full height again: they used to leave room up to the peak, which pressed the line into the bottom of the card whenever a quiet hour contained one short spike.

  • The system readings refresh faster

    The dashboard now updates them every 5 seconds instead of every 7. That is not an arbitrary number: the CPU temperature and graphics readings underneath are held for 5 seconds, so this is the quickest the dashboard can ask without the answer being a repeat of the one before. Nothing is read from your hardware any more often than it was, so it costs nothing extra. Asking genuinely faster than that would mean reading the sensors themselves more often, which is real work happening continuously, including while you are playing, so it is not something to switch on for everybody without saying so.

  • The Energy widget no longer explains, permanently, a reading your PC cannot give

    If your power supply has no chip to report its own output, and most do not, the widget said so in a line under the cards. It is true and it is worth knowing once, but there is nothing you can do about it without buying a different power supply, so it does not belong on a dashboard you are only looking at. It now appears while you are arranging the layout, where it explains the missing card to the person deciding what goes where. The message about Windows blocking access to the sensors is different and stays where it was, because that one you can fix with a click.

  • The Deck can let the dashboard show through it now

    The Deck is drawn as a solid object: a moulded body with a recessed well holding the keys. That stays the default, but it also means the Deck hides whatever is behind it, and on a dashboard with a picture background that is the one tile that always looks like a box. There is a Trasparenza slider in the Deck's Aspetto panel now. It fades the body and the well together, from the device you have today all the way to nothing but the keys floating over your background. The keys stay solid on purpose: a see-through cap loses its label the moment something bright passes behind it. The setting belongs to a Deck profile, so one profile can be a device and another can be bare keys, and it travels in a shared Deck code with the rest of the look. If the Deck shares a tile with other widgets as a tab, that tile paints itself as the device's mount for as long as the Deck is the open tab, and it now fades with it. This slider is the only thing that can make it see-through: while the Deck is showing, that paint takes the place of the tile's own opacity setting. The Nessuna faceplate removes it too, which it always should have: that finish exists to take the body away, and the mount was the same box under a different name, so choosing it left the box you were trying to get rid of. The tab bar stays as it is, because the tab names have to remain readable against whatever is behind them. The Fumetto and Retro themes draw their own body instead of the standard one, so the slider does not apply there.

  • Setting up your phone is now a guide inside Xenon, not a link to a website

    Settings → Telefono is a good set of switches and no help at all if you have never seen any of it, and the only ordered list of steps it had appeared *after* the secure connection had already failed. There is now a step-by-step guide in the panel, opened for you when you answer "my phone or tablet" on first run and reachable at any time from the button at the top. It walks you across the actual switches, in order: turn on access, scan the QR code, add it to your phone's home screen, and then, if you want it to work away from home too, the Tailscale half, install and sign in (Xenon does that part for you), turn on HTTPS certificates in your Tailscale account, which is the one step Xenon cannot do for you and nobody would guess, install Tailscale on the phone with the same account, and pair again on the new address. It knows which steps you have already done, so leaving and coming back lands you on the right one. In all 11 languages.

  • Choosing "my phone" no longer decides that your PC shows nothing

    It used to mean both things at once, and plenty of people want the dashboard on the phone *and* on the PC. Now it only says where you want the dashboard; at the end of the guide, once a phone is actually paired, Xenon asks whether it should keep opening on this PC as well, and does what you answer. Settings → Schermo has a fourth choice for it, Sul telefono e anche su questo PC, so you can change your mind either way at any time. If you do hide it, Xenon keeps running in the background so the phone carries on working, and the icon next to the clock brings the window back.

  • The first-run question about which screen to use arrives when the dashboard does, and nothing draws over it any more

    It was waiting for every image, font and widget frame on the page to finish loading, and then a further moment on top, so it appeared long after the dashboard looked finished. Worse, it could be covered: Xenon has one place that decides when something is allowed to interrupt you, and the first-run question and the guided tour were not listed in it. So a new arrival in the Store, which checks about twenty seconds after the dashboard loads, and an announcement, which checks about thirty-five, both found the screen free and drew straight over the one thing the app had asked you. The question now comes up as soon as the dashboard is ready, and nothing at all is allowed on top of it or of the tour. The "what's new" panel is in that same order too: it comes before any promotion, and on a brand-new install it does not appear at all, because there is no earlier version for it to tell you about.

  • A fresh install stops staring at a spinner for twenty seconds

    After the installer finishes, the app opens and waits for the part of Xenon that does the actual work. When that part was never installed, which is the case on every new PC, the app had no way of saying so and simply spun for twenty seconds before offering to finish the setup. It now checks, and offers within a couple of seconds.

  • Everything your phone does with Xenon is now in its own Settings section, called Telefono

    Phone access, the secure connection, notifications and the new file transfer had all been put under Controllo Remoto, and that was wrong: Controllo Remoto is the Sunshine and Moonlight wizard, which streams your PC's desktop and lets you drive it with a mouse from another country. Pairing a phone does none of that. Three separate things in one long scroll under a name that promised a fourth, so the section had stopped being a section. Controllo Remoto is now that wizard alone, and Telefono holds the phone door and what comes through it. The panel itself was tidied at the same time: the file-transfer block was running the full width of the settings window instead of staying in the same column as everything above it, the arrival folder was printed twice, once as a label and again inside the field under it, and its switches did not look like the switches ten pixels higher up. Usa questa cartella is now active only when you have actually changed the folder, and settings that do nothing while the feature is off no longer stay on screen asking to be filled in.

  • The website's home page has been rebuilt

    It had grown into fifteen sections built to the same recipe: a green label, a title at the same size every time, a paragraph, then a grid of translucent rounded cards. About forty of those cards in a row, which is a texture people now recognise on sight and read as a page nobody wrote. It is now ten numbered movements, each shaped differently from the one before it. The live figures (downloads, GitHub stars, Discord members) have moved above the fold, where they can do the job they are there for, and the ones that matter most are set in the same monospaced face as the rest of the page's labels. The features are one scene now instead of seven alternating blocks: the text scrolls and the screenshot beside it changes to match. The list of widgets is no longer fifteen examples but the whole set of 40, named exactly as the app names them. The widest slot on the page, the full-width one right after the five essentials, now goes to what the phone and the PC do for each other: files in both directions, a countdown that reaches a phone with its screen off, and the card that takes the screen when somebody calls you. RGB used to hold that slot and still has its own place further down, because it is a real feature that happens to need hardware most visitors do not own. And the thank-you section and the wall of supporters have become one movement, so the coffee button and the wall it puts your name on are finally in sight of each other, with the wall set as a plaque rather than a leaderboard of medals and pills.

  • Xenon stops describing itself as a Xeneon Edge accessory

    It was written when the Edge was the only screen it ran on, and the wording stuck: the welcome screen greeted every new user with "a dashboard built for your Xeneon Edge" in all eleven languages, including on a Mac with no Edge in the house; the native app was "dedicated to the Xeneon Edge"; the install steps on the website said Xenon opens on the Edge "or in any browser", in that order; and the README still said a phone or tablet was not possible, which stopped being true in this very release. All of it now says what is actually true: any screen you can spare, including the one in your pocket. The places that still name the panel are the ones genuinely about it, the preview at its exact 2560×720 and the hybrid-GPU note, and they are unchanged.

  • macOS, Linux and phone access now say they are beta, and say what that means

    All three are new in this release, and a version that does not admit which parts are new is a version that lets you find out by hitting one. Settings → Controllo Remoto carries a Beta mark next to Accesso dal telefono; on a Mac or a Linux machine the bottom of the Settings sidebar carries one too, next to the version, with a link to the table of what works where. The line under each mark is the important part: the dashboard, the widgets, the Store and the integrations are the same on every system, and what still differs is the part that reads the machine itself. In all 11 languages. On Windows nothing appears, because there is nothing true to say.

  • The website hands you the right download instead of assuming a PC

    It used to lead with the Windows installer and list the other two as small text, which is how a Mac visitor concludes there is no Mac build. There are now three cards, one per system, each with its own logo, its requirements and its own file: the one you are browsing from is marked Your OS and its button is the green one, and macOS and Linux carry the same Beta mark the app does. A fourth band under them covers the case the site was quietly losing: you do not need a second monitor at all, because your phone or tablet is one. Visit it from a phone and it says so, and points at the guide instead of offering you an .exe you cannot run.

  • Connecting YouTube is explained step by step

    The Settings → Streaming card compressed the whole Google Cloud setup into one sentence, and the one detail that actually blocks people (adding your own account as a test user, without which Google refuses the sign-in as "unverified app") read like an aside. The instructions are now four numbered steps, in all 11 languages, in the order the Google console actually presents things: enable the API, set up the consent screen and add yourself as a test user, create the "TVs and Limited Input devices" client, paste the two values and connect.

  • Your Gemini key stops leaving your PC

    It was the one AI key Xenon sent to the browser, and on a paired phone that meant sending it across your Wi-Fi in the clear, every time a page loaded. It turns out it never needed to go anywhere: every place the dashboard appeared to use the key was really handing it back to Xenon on your own PC, which is what talks to Google. So it does not travel any more. The settings field behaves like the ChatGPT and Claude ones, once saved it shows a row of dots instead of the key, with a Remove key button when you want it gone, and nothing else changes: the AI, the voice, the transcription, the performance advisor and the disk advisor all work exactly as they did, on the PC and on a paired tablet alike. A key you had already saved is moved over on its own the first time you open the dashboard; you do not have to enter it again.

  • A nearly sold-out limited drop no longer reads as a flop

    With 5 copies left of 50 the website said "5 / 50", which most people read as five *taken*: the exact opposite of the truth, and the worst possible thing to say about a drop that is almost gone. It now says "5 of 50 left", in your language, with the numbers in the order that language actually uses (Korean, Japanese and Chinese put the total first, and were wrong regardless of the reading).

  • Widget creators: the store's write limit is written down, and it was quietly costing data

    A widget's persistent store accepts one write every 100 milliseconds per package. A write arriving inside that window is answered rate_limited and stores nothing, which was documented nowhere: a widget saving several keys at once (a game saving its progress and its statistics together, a settings panel saving four fields on one tap) kept the first and lost the rest, with no sign anything had gone wrong until the next load came back empty. docs/WIDGET_SDK.md now states the limit next to the size caps, shows a small queue that spaces writes out and retries a refusal, and says plainly that the result of a write has to be checked.

  • Community widgets can now follow the Pixel Retro skin, not just your colours

    A widget was told your palette but never which of Xenon's two looks was on, and the two differ in shape rather than colour: Pixel Retro is square corners, thick borders, hard shadows with no blur and a monospace face. So a widget could follow your theme perfectly and still sit in a pixel dashboard looking like a pane of glass. It is now told which skin is running, on install and on every theme change, with the exact recipe written down for creators so they mirror the real thing instead of guessing at it. Nothing is granted by this and nothing about you is shared; it is one word describing what is already on your screen.

  • Widget creators: three gaps in the SDK are closed

    expand is documented in docs/WIDGET_SDK.md with the exact rules the host enforces and the errors you get back. init now carries service: true|false, so a package that runs both a hidden background frame and a tile can finally tell which copy of itself is speaking instead of guessing, and keep its side effects in exactly one of them. And the documentation now says that a widget can play sound, which was true all along and written down nowhere: bundled clips or synthesised tones both work, with the rules that matter written next to them (a tap is needed to start, default to silent, go quiet when nobody is looking).

  • The website has an FAQ, and it starts with the thing that stops people: Windows calling Xenon a virus

    Until now the only explanation lived in the README, so the two questions that come up most on the Discord had no page to point at. xenon-app.com/faq.html covers both, in all five languages of the site. The first is Defender quarantining the app: why the !cl in the detection name means the verdict came from a cloud model and not from matching real malware, how to get your install back, and how to check the file's hash yourself so you are not taking anyone's word for it. The second is new here and was missing everywhere: Smart App Control, which is a separate system from your antivirus, is not affected by an antivirus exclusion, and cannot be told to allow one app. It is also worth knowing before you touch it that switching it off cannot be undone without reinstalling Windows, and that is now said plainly instead of being discovered afterwards. Around those sit the rest of what gets asked: whether you need a Xeneon Edge, what beta means on macOS and Linux, macOS refusing to open an app Apple cannot check, Full Disk Access, updating, uninstalling, the AI key, privacy, and the licence. The README gained the Smart App Control section too.

  • The floating row of page dots at the bottom of the screen has been removed

    It was added to help when a widget fills the whole page and a swipe cannot start, but it duplicated the page dots that already sit in the top bar, so it was more clutter than help. Page switching stays where it always was: tap the dots in the top bar to move between pages, and if you want to swipe with a finger, leave a little room around a full-page widget so there is background to start the gesture on.

Fixes

  • A widget that opens a page in the Browser tile now works when the tile is not already on screen

    Widgets from the Store can hand an address to your Browser tile, so a map, a wiki or a dashboard opens on your screen instead of on your desktop. It only worked if the Browser tile happened to be visible at that moment, and the arrangement most people build is the one where it never is: the widget and the Browser put together as two tabs of a single tile, which is how you fit two large things on the Xeneon Edge. Being two tabs of the same tile means they can never be on screen at the same time, so every attempt came back as "no Browser tile" and the widget fell back to opening the page in your normal browser, on your desktop, which is the one thing the feature exists to avoid. Xenon now brings a Browser tile into view first: it switches to that tab, or scrolls to the page it lives on, preferring one already on the page you are looking at so it changes as little as possible. The tile is still never replaced behind your back, which is why it was refusing in the first place. If your dashboard has no Browser tile at all, the widget is told so and can say it, as before. Reported on the forum by a widget author whose map explorer could not reach the Browser sitting next to it.

  • Performance Mode's per-app CPU figures were slightly wrong, in a way nothing could report

    The optimization sheet and the AI planner read how much processor time each app had used over a short sample. A quirk of how that sample was clamped meant every app's figure was rounded down to a whole millisecond before being counted, so the numbers were consistently a little under the truth and the smallest consumers could vanish entirely. Nothing errored and nothing looked broken; the figures were simply not what they said they were. They are now measured at full precision.

  • "Detail unavailable" under a disk no longer sticks for ten minutes at a time

    The line under a drive in the System widget shows its volume name, file system and type, and it came from a group of three Windows queries that Xenon gave five seconds to answer between them. Those queries go through the part of Windows that reports storage, which is often slower than five seconds the first time it is asked after a restart. When they ran out of time, Xenon wrote down "no details" as if it were the answer and kept it for ten minutes before asking again, so the line stayed empty long enough to look permanent, and restarting made it worse rather than better because a restart is exactly when those queries are slowest. Three things changed. A read that comes back with nothing is now treated as a failed read: it is retried within the minute, and it never replaces details Xenon already had. Every read after the first happens in the background with the time the queries actually need, so the panel fills in on its own instead of waiting. And the query that the line is actually built from has been separated from the two that are not: only one of the three is needed for the name, file system and type, while the other two exist to name the physical disk, which nothing on screen is waiting for. They now run on their own and cannot cost you a line that was already answerable. The user who reported this measured the fast query at half a second on his own PC while his card still read "Detail unavailable", which is what pointed at the other two. The fallback Xenon uses on PCs where the modern query is not available is also protected properly now. Reported on Discord.

  • A drive with no name now shows the disk it is on, instead of just "NTFS - Fixed"

    Most Windows volumes carry no label, because nothing asks you to give one, so the line under a drive in the System widget was left saying only the file system and the type: true, and of no use to anybody. When there is no label, that line now names the disk itself, so it reads something like "Samsung SSD 990 PRO - NTFS - Fixed". Xenon was already reading that name for the Storage widget and simply was not showing it here. A drive you have named still shows your name for it, as before.

  • A Deck key made by pasting a path copied from Explorer now opens the app

    Windows' own "Copy as path" wraps the path in quotation marks, and pasting that straight into a key is the natural way to set one up. Xenon took the quotation marks as part of the file name, so it looked for a file that does not exist, gave up, and the key flashed red on every press with a path in the editor that looked exactly right. Nothing on screen pointed at the quotation marks. They are now removed when the key is saved, for opening an app, opening a file and running a script, and a key you already made this way starts working on the next press without you having to touch it. A path without quotation marks is left alone, as is a file whose name genuinely contains one. Reported on Discord by a user whose Deck app keys had never opened anything.

  • A round widget is round again, instead of being squashed into an oval with a band around it

    Any widget from the Store that gives itself a circular shape could be cut to an ellipse instead of a circle, with a band all the way round it: pale on a dark theme, bright white on a light one, and worst on a page you had to swipe to. Xenon was working the shape's proportions out from the size of the tile and keeping the answer, and that measurement could be taken while the layout was still moving, or while the page was put away and the tile collapsed, and once taken it was never revisited, because nothing about the tile changed afterwards. Measured on a real install: a tile whose circle needed one proportion was carrying another four times off. A circle is now left to the browser, which works it out against the tile on every frame and cannot be caught at the wrong moment. Shapes that are not circles also measure the box the shape is actually cut from, and are measured again when a page comes back or the window changes size.

  • The file index no longer rebuilds itself over and over, eating a processor core for as long as the PC is on

    If you had the Living Index switched on, xenon-helper could sit at around 20% CPU and swing between 400 MB and 1.4 GB of memory forever, deflating and climbing back. It was not a peak and it was not finishing: measured on a real install, the index was re-reading the whole of C: end to end roughly every twenty seconds, for hours. Each pass also threw away what it had and started from nothing, so at any moment the search and the Disk widget could be looking at a quarter of your files without either of them being able to tell. The cause was the recovery, not the fault: when the operating system tells Xenon "you have missed some file changes", Xenon re-read the whole drive, and re-reading the drive held the index busy long enough to miss more changes, which asked for another re-read. It could not stop. Three things changed. Xenon now takes note of a changed file and moves on instead of doing the work while the operating system waits, which is what kept it missing changes in the first place. When a re-read is genuinely needed it updates in place and removes only what it confirms is gone, so the index is never emptied and neither the search nor the disk map goes blind. And a re-read waits for the disk to go quiet and happens at most once every ten minutes per drive, so no amount of file activity can turn into a permanent rebuild. Deleting a folder no longer rebuilds an internal table of every indexed file either, which build tools were triggering hundreds of times in a row.

  • Installing Xenon from inside the zip window no longer produces an install that breaks weeks later

    Double-clicking the downloaded zip in Explorer does not unpack it: Windows shows you the contents and, if you start INSTALL.bat from there, quietly copies everything into a temporary folder first. The install worked, the dashboard came up, and everything ran normally for as long as that folder survived. Then Windows cleared its temporary files, and the next sign-in showed "Can not find script file" and a dashboard waiting for a service that no longer existed anywhere on the disk. Your settings, notes and layout went with the folder. The installer now recognises that it is running from a temporary location before it installs anything, copies Xenon to a permanent folder of its own (AppData\Local\Programs\Xenon, the same place the app's own setup uses), and carries on from there. If it cannot, it stops and tells you to extract the zip yourself instead of installing something that will disappear. Reported on Discord by someone whose install had been running fine for weeks.

  • A Performance Mode session you started by hand no longer stays on forever

    Switching it on for a game and finding it still running hours later was easy to do and almost impossible to notice, because the symptom is that the dashboard goes quiet: animations paused everywhere, nothing on screen saying why, and no reason to go looking in Performance settings for it. Sessions Xenon starts by itself have always ended by themselves when you stopped playing; one you started yourself had no ending at all. It has one now, and it is the session's own: Xenon remembers which app the session was started for, and when that app is gone the session ends and puts back what it changed, with the same notification an automatic one gives. It asks Windows directly whether that app is still running, and asks twice, half a minute apart, so an app that is merely restarting does not cost you the session; an answer that does not come back never counts as evidence. A session you started without any particular app in mind is left alone, that one is still yours to switch off, and so is every session on macOS and Linux, where the check Windows answers does not exist. Found while working out why a mascot in the top bar was standing still: the answer was a session started for a game that had been closed long before.

  • Settings → Performance no longer opens on a "Hardware sensors" panel with nothing in it

    That section exists for one job: when Xenon was installed without administrator rights, CPU temperature, fan speeds and watts can never be read, and it offers the one-click repair. But the panel was always there whatever the answer was, so it did the opposite of its job twice over. On a PC where the sensors work it sat at the very top of the page, above Performance Mode, which is what people open that page for, saying only "Hardware sensors are already on", which reads as a heading somebody forgot to fill in. And on macOS and Linux, where the software those sensors need does not exist at all, it drew a titled panel that was completely empty, announcing a subject and then having nothing to say about it. The section now appears only when there is something to repair, and brings its heading with it. Nothing changes for anyone who does have the problem: the same explanation and the same button, in the same place.

  • A Storico chart whose sensor had been unavailable drew a short line adrift in its own card

    The charts reserved width for every hour in the range, including the hours a reading never arrived in, so a metric that is not always available drew a stub in the middle of an otherwise empty card, with a break through it. The CPU temperature does this routinely: it needs LibreHardwareMonitor running, and while that is not up the hour is recorded with nothing in it. Those charts now use the readings that exist, side by side, filling the card. The labels along the bottom say which hours they are, and when the readings run across midnight the two ends carry their date, so a chart reading 13h on the left and 16h on the right cannot be mistaken for three hours.

  • A community widget in a tab group was labelled "Custom widget" instead of its own name

    The tab takes the name of the widget you assign to the tile, and it was being worked out when the list of installed widgets loads, which is not the moment that decides it. Assigning a widget to the tile repaints the tile without rebuilding the tab bar, so the tab kept the generic name until the next reload, and after removing a widget it kept naming one that was no longer there. The label now follows the assignment, including when it is made from another screen.

  • Pasting your unlock code into the import box said "not a valid preset code" and left you there

    A limited drop arrives as two things: a personal file to download and a personal code to open it with. The Store's I have a code button opens the import dialog empty, so the natural thing to do is paste the code you were just given, which is the one thing that box cannot take. The answer was a dead end with no next step. Xenon now recognises a code of its own and tells you what to do with it: open the download link you were sent, choose the .json file, and the unlock field appears with your code's place in it. In all 11 languages.

  • On Windows, "show in folder" opened your Documents folder instead of the file you asked about

    It happened whenever the path contained a space, which is almost every path, so for most people the button never once did what it says. Both places that offer it were affected: the search results and the file-transfer widget. The folder that opened was unrelated to anything you had clicked, and nothing reported a problem, so it read as Xenon losing track of your files. Windows Explorer is fussy about how it is asked to highlight a file, and Xenon was asking in a way it quietly gives up on. It now opens the right folder with the file already selected.

  • The storage panel and the Claude Code panel were in English whichever language you had chosen

    Both were written in Italian and English only, and the other nine languages fell back to English without saying so, which looks like a translation you have not noticed rather than one that was never there. For the storage panel that included every line explaining what Xenon will and will not delete, which is the last place a user should be reading a language they did not pick. Both panels are now written in all 11 languages. Korean, Japanese, Chinese and Dutch turned out to have some of the Claude text already translated under names the app had stopped using, so those translations existed and could never appear; they are back in use.

  • Ten pieces of text could not be translated at all, in any language, Italian included

    The code asked for them by name and that name was defined nowhere, so each one fell back to a fixed English sentence built into the code. Among them: "No upcoming events" on the ambient screen, "Community widgets are turned off", both lines describing what a community widget may do when it fills the screen, and the unlock-code field in the redeem dialog. All ten now exist in all 11 languages.

  • The Deck's "Ask Claude" key called its text box "Prompt" when it should have said "Request"

    The right wording had been written, but it shared a name with the Xenon AI key's own label, so whichever was read last replaced the other and the intended one could never appear. The two keys can now label their boxes separately, and nothing about existing Deck keys changes.

  • On Fedora, Arch, openSUSE, RHEL and Manjaro, no USB stick or external drive appeared in the Disks widget

    Those systems mount removable media under /run/media, and Xenon was skipping everything under /run because most of what lives there is not a real disk. The result was a Disks widget that showed only the system drive, on the very machines where plugging something in is the reason to look at it. Ubuntu and Debian were unaffected, which is why it went unnoticed. Drives whose name contains a space (My Passport) were also being dropped, for a separate reason in the same place, and are back too.

  • On Linux, the backend never started again after the first restart if Xenon was installed in a folder with a space in its name

    The login service was written as one line of text and the system reads it up to the first space, so /home/you/My Apps/xenon became a path that does not exist. The install itself worked, because that part started the server a different way, so the problem only showed up at the next reboot, with no message anywhere. The service is now written so a space is just a space, and the installer checks that the server really survived being started rather than assuming it did.

  • Changing one app's volume on Linux could change every app's volume

    If the app name arrived empty (which the dashboard could do in a couple of places), the match that finds "the app called X" matched everything instead of nothing. Muting one thing muted the machine. An empty name now matches nothing and says so.

  • On a Mac, the Deck's keyboard shortcuts and the global search hotkey stayed unavailable no matter what

    Re-running the installer is how the Mac companion updates, and the installer was still asking for a version older than the one that added those abilities, so it decided the copy on disk was new enough and left it alone. Existing Mac installs were stuck on it permanently.

  • File-transfer limits went back to their defaults every time Xenon started

    The maximum file size, the storage cap and how long files are kept were read before your settings had been loaded, so a limit you had raised applied only until the next restart, and then quietly stopped applying. Sending a large file failed with a limit you thought you had changed. They are now read from your settings at startup, and after restoring a backup.

  • On Linux, search and the disk map could stay on "indexing" forever

    The index is rebuilt on a timer, and the timer did not check whether the previous rebuild had finished. On a large home folder, or one on a network drive, every tick threw away the work in progress and started from zero, so the index never finished, search never returned anything, and the disk stayed busy the whole time. A rebuild that is still running is now left to finish.

  • On a Mac, restarting Xenon from the tray left the old dashboard server running

    Restarting replaces the app in place, and the step that stops the server it started was tied to a shutdown that a restart skips. The abandoned server kept the port, so the new copy never took ownership of it, and quitting later left it running with nothing on screen. Every restart path now stops the server first.

  • Choosing "on my phone or tablet" while the app was collapsed to the round button left it stuck as the round button

    With no way back: the button did nothing, "Show Xenon" did not undo it, and only closing the app from the task manager got out of it. Coming back from the desktop now always restores a normal window, whichever screen setting you are on.

  • Your screen choice could be forgotten after a crash, and the login entry came back with it

    The preference file was deleted a moment before the new one was put in its place, which was never necessary, and anything that interrupted Xenon in that instant left it with no file to read. It then started as if you had never chosen anything, including switching automatic start back on for someone who had turned it off. The old file is now replaced in one step, and the new one is on disk before it is used.

  • On a minimal Linux install, updating could fail every time and never say why

    Stopping the running server relies on one of two standard tools to find it, and where neither was present nothing was stopped, the update was applied around a server that was still running, and Xenon then decided the update had not worked and rolled it back. Every attempt after that did the same. There is now a third way to find it that needs no extra tools at all.

  • On a Mac or Linux, moving or deleting the Xenon folder left the app opening a terminal window at every launch, to tell you nothing was wrong

    The window is the one that finishes an install, and it decided the install was already complete because a leftover startup entry was still there, without checking whether anything it pointed at still existed. It now checks, and finishes the install instead.

  • A page you merely visited could burn through your YouTube quota

    The live-chat reading was reachable from any website in a way the rest of the YouTube integration is not, and the answer it holds on to is kept per page of chat, so a page asking for a different one each time went straight through to YouTube. A few thousand of those would have left your own YouTube widget dead for the rest of the day. It is now protected the same way the search is, and asking for chat while you are not live no longer costs anything.

  • Xenon on a phone could open on the pairing screen when it could not reach your PC, instead of saying so

    The copy it keeps for that moment is meant to be the dashboard, but if the page had been saved while the phone was waiting to be paired, the pairing screen was saved instead, and that is what came up. Only the dashboard is kept now.

  • On Linux, "Show in folder" could take the whole dashboard down

    On a system without a file manager installed, the failure was of a kind Xenon could not catch, and it ended the server rather than the action. From a paired phone that was one tap.

  • On a Mac, setting up secure phone access stopped at "Tailscale is not running" and went no further

    The step that starts the background service has nothing to start on a Mac, where the Tailscale app is the service, and the step that knows to open the app came after it and was never reached. The setup now moves on to it.

  • A global search shortcut on GNOME could be accepted and then never work

    Xenon checks whether the combination you picked is already taken, but only recognised one way of writing it, and the desktop writes it several. A conflict spelled differently slipped through, and GNOME resolves two shortcuts on the same keys by running neither. The check now understands all of them.

  • Restoring a backup made on another PC sent your incoming files to a folder that does not exist here

    The bundle carries the folder you chose for phone transfers, which is a path on the machine it was taken from, and the import was preferring it over the one set on this PC. The folder is now always the one this machine already had. It can still be changed where it always could, in Settings, from the PC.

  • Half of the Settings panels had stopped appearing

    Paired devices, file transfer, the Sunshine wizard, Streaming, Spotify, Smart Home, Cameras, the lighting hub and the external-calendar section all rendered as an empty page. They are built one after another by the same routine, and a few lines above them that routine was reading your theme's panel colour, which was not a colour any more: the screen you pick when Xenon first opens was being saved under the same name as that colour, in the same place, so every save overwrote one with the other. Nothing complained at the point where it happened. It broke much later, in a routine that expected a colour, and everything queued behind it never ran. The screen choice now has a name of its own, the colour is a colour again, and the screen you already picked is carried across, so Xenon will not ask you again. If you had set a custom panel colour, it is back to automatic and needs setting once more.

  • Anything smaller than a megabyte was shown as a raw number of bytes

    A photo from your phone read 584625 B instead of 571 KB, because the size formatter the whole dashboard shares went straight from megabytes down to bytes with no kilobyte step in between. It had never been visible before: the widgets that show sizes show memory and disks, and those are always megabytes and up. The file list was the first place small files appear, and it appeared on the very first row. Sizes under a kilobyte are still shown in bytes, where a plain number is still readable.

  • The file-transfer tile has been redrawn

    It came out functional and unfinished. The two buttons said "Foto e video" and "Altri file" with nothing to say they add anything, so they read as a pair of tabs; everything below the last file was bare wallpaper with no edge to it; nothing ever mentioned that you can drag files onto the tile, because the only thing that did was a dashed area shown when the list was empty, which is exactly when nobody is looking; and the heading was set in a dim uppercase that no other widget on the dashboard uses. Now the list takes the room it needs and everything left over is one panel that says you can drop files there and holds the two pickers, each with the icon of what it opens. The heading matches the other tiles, and how much has been stored sits beside it as a small badge. Files that came from a phone and files you put there from the PC are told apart by a mark on the thumbnail instead of by two words at the end of the dimmest line in the row.

  • The first-run tutorial sometimes never appeared, and it was a coin toss

    The tour is offered once the saved settings have been read back from the PC, and that read is started by a script near the top of the page while the tour's own script is about eighty script tags further down. Reading the settings is a request to your own machine and can answer in a couple of milliseconds, faster, sometimes, than the browser gets to the rest of the page. When it won that race the tour simply was not loaded yet, so nothing was offered and nothing said so; when it lost, the tour appeared as intended. Same page, same install, different outcome depending on how busy the machine was that second. The offer now waits until the page has finished loading, so it no longer depends on who was faster.

  • Settings now says plainly how to switch file indexing off, and shows you that it is off

    The line under the index list said the whole C:\ was there by default and, in the same breath, that emptying the list turns the index off, which read as a contradiction: does a list you clear stay clear, or does the drive come back? It stays clear. The default only applies until the first time you edit the list, and the text says that now, in all 11 languages. With the list empty, the status line under it no longer disappears: it reads that the living index is off, that Xenon is indexing nothing, and that the Disk space widget's map goes empty too, since it reads those same drives and folders. On Windows the same note adds the part people ask about next: search keeps working with the index off, because it also reads Windows' own search catalog, which Microsoft maintains whether Xenon is installed or not and which Xenon only queries. If you want nothing at all indexing your files, that one is turned off in Windows itself, not here. Separately, nine languages were still showing the pre-v4.10 wording for this setting ("extra folders to index") because an older copy of the text was overriding the current one, and the Italian and English lines had lost the backslashes in their C:\ and D:\Archivio examples.

  • The download counter on the website was about to stop counting

    It added up every release file whose name contained "setup", which was every installer there had ever been while Windows was the only system. From this release the Mac and Linux builds are .dmg, .AppImage and .deb files, none of which say "setup", so the figure on the home page would have kept reporting Windows alone and looked frozen while downloads carried on. All four installers are counted now. The helper is still left out on purpose: every install pulls it and every update pulls it again, so counting it would say something about updates rather than about people installing Xenon.

  • Two parts of the website stayed in English whatever language you chose

    The exclusive-drops cards ("Supporters only", "5 of 50 left", "Claim your copy") and the ranks on the wall of supporters ("Top supporter", "2nd place") were written once when the page loaded and never touched again, so switching language changed everything around them and left them behind. Both are rebuilt when you switch now, and the three ranks exist in all five languages instead of only English.

  • Settings could not be read at all, and it turned phone access off without telling anyone

    One card in the YouTube widget was listed but had no default, and the settings file is rebuilt from those defaults every time it is read, so reading it failed outright. Xenon fell back to factory settings in memory while your real file sat on disk, untouched and correct. Everything the browser saves survived, because the browser keeps its own copy; what did not survive was the handful of settings only the server holds. Phone access is one of them, so a phone that had been working for hours started getting the same flat refusal as a version of Xenon that never had the feature, while the panel on the PC still showed the switch as on. Fixed, and the check that already existed for widgets now covers cards too, this is the second time this exact gap has cost a release, and it cannot happen a third time silently.

  • Every Store widget was unreadable on an iPhone or iPad

    They came up as plain black text on a white rectangle, with none of their own design, while the same widget on the same Wi-Fi looked perfect on a PC. The cause was one word in a security header. Widgets run in a locked-down frame with no identity of their own, and the rule that let a widget load its own stylesheet said "same place as this page", which, for a frame with no identity, means nowhere. Chrome and Edge quietly read it the lenient way; Safari reads it the way it is written, and blocked every widget's stylesheet and script. Since every other screen Xenon runs on is Chrome-based (the Xeneon Edge, the desktop app, desktop browsers), the bug could only ever appear on an iPhone or an iPad. Xenon now says which place it means, so both readings agree. Nothing was loosened: widgets still have no network at all.

  • Widgets came up as white boxes on a paired phone, and reloading made it worse

    A paired device had a budget of 900 requests a minute, and loading the dashboard costs 250 of them, the shell alone is over two hundred files. So the fourth reload inside a minute started being refused, and what a page asks for last is exactly the widgets' own stylesheets and scripts: the dashboard came up looking perfectly healthy with its widgets rendered as bare text on a white background. It looked like a broken widget, so the natural next move was to reload, which spent more of the same budget and guaranteed it happened again. The budget is now written as a multiple of what a real load costs, with room for two dozen of them a minute, and a test keeps it there. Nothing about what a paired device is allowed to reach has changed.

  • The phone guide is now linked from inside Xenon

    Settings → Controllo Remoto carries a link to the full walkthrough at xenon-app.com/phone.html, in all 11 languages, and it is there in the two states where the panel says least: before you switch anything on, and on a paired phone, where the pairing controls are closed by design.

  • The Browser tile could be left with the page filling only part of it, and only "Show toolbar" put it right

    Hiding the toolbar gives the page the space the toolbar was using, and the tile tells the page its new size so it re-renders to fit. That message was sent and then simply assumed to have worked: if it was lost, or if the one repaint it asks for was taken while the page was still rearranging itself, the tile kept showing the page at the old size. Nothing ever noticed, because a page that has stopped changing sends nothing new, so it stayed that way until something resized the tile again, which is why showing the toolbar back appeared to be the cure. The tile now checks. Every frame the page sends says which size it was drawn at, the tile compares it against the size it asked for, and asks again when they disagree; if a resize produces no frame at all, it is retried a few times and then left alone rather than looped on forever. Hiding or showing the toolbar also pushes the new size immediately instead of waiting for the browser to notice the tile changed shape, and the page is given a second chance to repaint once it has settled. Reported on GitHub as issue #116.

  • Searching for a short common word found nothing

    Xenon's search understands whole sentences, "trovami i file di marci di questo mese", and to do that it ignores the words that carry no meaning: articles, prepositions, "trova", "apri", "the", "my". That is right for a sentence and wrong for a single word, because the moment you typed just ma, or in, or my, the only thing you had written was thrown away and the search answered "no results" while you were still typing. A one-word query is now searched for as you wrote it. Sentences are unchanged, and a word that means something to the search, foto, .pdf, still filters instead of being looked for by name.

  • The news feeds you follow can be changed from Settings, not only from the News widget

    The outlets, topics and RSS feeds behind the news were editable in one place: the gear button in the News widget's own header. That is fine while the widget is on your dashboard, but the scrolling ticker shows news without needing the widget at all, so anyone using the ticker on its own had headlines arriving with no way anywhere to change where they came from. Settings → Borsa, Calcio e News → News now holds the same editor: search an outlet, type a topic, or paste an RSS address, and remove what you no longer want from the same chips. It is the same list the widget shows, so a change in one place is immediately the change in the other. Worth knowing if the default feeds are not in your language: Xenon ships with ANSA, BBC News and the topic "tecnologia", and free topics follow the language the dashboard is set to.

  • Windows should stop deleting Xenon

    Defender had started quarantining xenon-native.exe as Trojan:Win32/Sonbokli.A!cl and refusing to let the new version download at all. Nothing was ever wrong with the code, that detection comes from Defender's cloud machine-learning model, not from a signature, but the way the setup behaved gave the model every reason to fire. Once it finished, the setup silently launched a hidden PowerShell window that downloaded the dashboard engine and ran it, and that shape, an unsigned installer starting an invisible downloader, next to a startup registry entry and a scheduled task, is exactly what a dropper does. Now nothing runs on its own: the setup installs the app and stops there, and if the app then finds no dashboard engine on the PC it says so on its startup screen and offers a Complete setup button. The install is the same one as before, byte for byte, except you start it and you watch it happen in a window you can see. Pressing the button when the engine is in fact already there is harmless, it checks and exits. This is a mitigation, not a cure: the real fix is a code-signing certificate, and until Xenon has one a fresh release can still be flagged. The README now explains how to check the download's signed SHA-256 hash and restore the file if Windows has taken it, and how to report the false positive to Microsoft, user reports are what get these detections withdrawn.

  • Settings on a phone showed nothing but its own category list

    All twenty-seven categories were laid out as a wrapping row of chips, which on a 390px screen is thirteen rows: they filled the screen from the title to the bottom, and the settings themselves were squeezed to no height at all, so opening Settings from a paired phone gave you a list and no way to see what any of it does. The three dividers that group the list (Widget, Integrazioni, Sistema) sat inline between two chips wherever the wrap happened to fall, which made the grouping read as noise rather than structure. On a narrow screen the list is now a picker: it shows the category you are in, so the settings are on screen where they belong, and tapping it opens the full list in two columns with the dividers on their own lines and each category readable in full instead of cut off with an ellipsis. Picking one closes it again. The list scrolls on its own, so the categories at the bottom can be reached, which they could not before: they were not pushed off the screen, they were cut off by the panel with nothing to scroll. Nothing changes on a monitor or on the Xeneon Edge, where the sidebar is unchanged. Separately, a category that does not exist on your system (the Windows-only ones, on a Mac or on Linux) was still listed and still opened an empty panel: it is hidden now, as it was always meant to be.

  • A limited drop you already own can be unlocked again after it sells out, which is what changing computer needs

    A copy of a limited edition is yours permanently: the code you were given works on up to three machines, and it has never had an expiry date. The Store did not say so. Once the last copy was claimed, or the drop closed, the whole panel was replaced by a "Sold out" label, and the I have a code button went with it, at exactly the moment it was the only thing that could help. So somebody who had bought a drop, changed PC, and come back to install it found a page that looked like a door shut in their face, even though their code would have been accepted. That button now stays on a sold-out and on a closed drop, next to the label saying no new copies are coming. Nothing about who may unlock what has changed, and there was never a limit to lift: this is the way back in becoming visible again.
